      <title>Fake film deals and emails from top agents: who is behind the explosion in literary scams?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/29/paid-for-book-clubs-fake-film-deals-emails-explosion-literary-scams-authors</link>
      <description><p>Writers are being bombarded daily with invitations from fake book groups and offers to publicise their work. For the scamming industry, aspiring authors can be a soft touch<br><br>• <strong>This piece first appeared in </strong><a href="https://www.thedial.world/articles/news/ai-book-scams"><strong>the Dial</strong></a></p><p>‘Hello Professor Snigdha Poonam,” the email began. I read that again. Nobody has ever called me “professor” for the obvious reason that I am not a professor. Bracing myself, I read on. The email was from Timothy Firth, organiser of a Seattle-based life-drawing community with 1,943 members that regularly has “thoughtful discussions inspired by creative works”. A recent inspiration was my first book, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/2018/feb/04/dreamers-how-young-indians-changed-the-world-review-snigdha-poonam">Dreamers: How Young Indians Are Changing Their World</a>. The group wanted to discuss it, the email said, at one of its upcoming meetups. Attendees would be encouraged to post reviews on Goodreads and Amazon after.</p><p>I looked up CAM Life Drawing and found an events page and an Instagram account. The latter had some photos of Timothy Firth – white, male – as well as testimonials from members who said he worked “day and night to create more community space”. Something told me this wasn’t the man who had reached out to me.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/29/paid-for-book-clubs-fake-film-deals-emails-explosion-literary-scams-authors">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Film buffs love it. Trump and Tom Hanks hosted it. Can TCM survive a Hollywood mega-merger?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/film/ng-interactive/2026/oct/28/turner-classic-movies-skydance-merger</link>
      <description><p>Since 1994, Turner Classic Movies has been a haven for old film lovers. Now with Skydance’s David Ellison calling the shots, fans are panicking over its unclear future</p><p>I have made many attempts to lessen the existential disaster we call Tuesday – tacos, trivia – but lately only one thing works. Every night just before 8pm, I hide my phone under a pillow in the next room, plate up a carb-heavy dinner, and turn on Turner Classic Movies (TCM) for Sweater Weather, a series of films dedicated to the transitional season.</p><p>Every Tuesday in October, Alicia Malone, an affable Australian film historian wearing business casual and a flippy bob, introduces a double feature. These are often midcentury melodramas featuring striking leads, serpentine plots, and the burnt hues of fall rendered in indulgent Technicolor. Like All That Heaven Allows (1955), about a widow who finds herself crushed under the weight of 1950s suburban conformity – and the teeny waistline of her swing skirts – while nursing a crush on her much-younger gardener. Or Leave Her to Heaven (1945), about a beautiful socialite so obsessed with her hapless husband that she will kill anyone who threatens their bond.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/ng-interactive/2026/oct/28/turner-classic-movies-skydance-merger">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Chancellor fleshes out details of scheme unveiled last month to help 70,000 households on to the property ladder</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/oct/28/budget-2026-key-points-john-healey">Budget 2026: key points at a glance</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/ng-interactive/2026/oct/28/budget-income-tax-thresholds-frozen-take-home-pay">Income tax: How much more will you pay?</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/sep/28/labour-help-to-buy-your-first-home">Nils Pratley: Labour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a try</a></p></li></ul><p></p><p></p><p>A new £4.7bn government scheme will help 70,000 households on to the property ladder and save first-time buyers “hundreds of pounds a month”, the chancellor, John Healey, said on Wednesday.</p><p>Last month, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/sep/26/andy-burnham-announces-new-scheme-for-first-time-home-buyers-england">Andy Burnham announced Your First Home</a>, which aims to give a helping hand to first-time buyers in England who do not have access to the “bank of mum and dad”, and Healey revealed in his first budget how the scheme would work, including who would be eligible.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/sep/28/first-home-scheme-first-time-buyers-what-you-need-to-know">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 29 Oct 2026 21:17:09 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Alphabet shares tumble in $500bn rout]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/29/alphabet-stock-sinks-as-search-woes-cause-revenue-miss/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/10/29/alphabet-stock-sinks-as-search-woes-cause-revenue-miss/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 15:42:23 +0000Alphabet shares tumbled 13 per cent on Thursday, wiping a record $500 billion (€443 billion) from its market value, after the Google owner burned through cash last quarter and revealed that “AI mode” searches were threatening profits at its core advertising business.

The plunge in the stock reverberated across markets, as the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 1.4 per cent in early trading.

If the decline holds through to the close of trading, it would represent the second-biggest daily drop in market value in Wall Street history, after Nvidia’s $593 billion rout in January 2025.

The Silicon Valley group’s cash flow fell deeper into negative territory in the three months to the end of September, reaching minus $9.1 billion, as it lifted its AI spending to more than $50 billion in the quarter.

The figure, which surpassed analysts’ forecasts, marked only the second quarter of negative cash flow since Google went public in 2004. It also comes as investors grow increasingly wary of whether the historic AI investment boom will pay off.

Analysts also flagged weakness in Google’s core search advertising business in third-quarter results that Alphabet released after the stock market closed on Wednesday.

Revenue in its largest division increased 12 per cent year on year to $63.4 billion, missing estimates for $64.9 billion and slowing from a near 20 per cent annual growth rate earlier in the year.

Philipp Schindler, chief business officer at Google, admitted ‘AI mode’ queries – which provide conversational text answers rather than a list of links – were eating into traditional search and led to “lower monetisation” via ads.

“Search is where the concern sits,” said David Wagner, head of equities at Aptus Capital Advisors. “In a market worried about AI chatbots cannibalising its key franchise, investors need to see it accelerating, not decelerating.”

The shift to burning cash has been caused by historic capital expenditure on AI as Alphabet makes an all-in bet on the transformational potential of the nascent technology.

Capex grew to $51.3 billion in the quarter, up from $44.9 billion in the second quarter. Chief financial officer Anat Ashkenazi reiterated that capex would reach as much as $205 billion this year, implying that spending in the fourth quarter could be as high as $73.1 billion.

Google disclosed it has made future commitments for data centre purchases, leases, equipment, energy and other obligations in excess of $1 trillion.

To back the spending spree, Alphabet has taken on tens of billions in debt and in June announced plans to raise about $85 billion in its first share sale in more than two decades – a sharp reversal after years of buying back its own shares.

In contrast, Microsoft received a warmer reception after strong growth in its Azure cloud unit helped revenue and profit beat estimates. While capex rose to $45.2 billion, the company still reported free cash flow of $18.6 billion.

Microsoft shares were 1 per cent higher in early trading on Thursday.

“Markets are carefully calibrating the trade-off between capex and free cash flow,” said Dec Mullarkey, managing director at asset management firm SLC Management. “Microsoft is a standout on cash discipline, while delivering on growth. Google fell short, and cash flow is expected to be a drag through next year.”

Alphabet’s revenue increased 25 per cent to $127.6 billion in the quarter, also falling slightly short of the average analyst forecast compiled by Factset.

Net income fell 25 per cent to $26.2 billion compared with the same period a year earlier, far from analysts’ expectations of $37.3 billion.

That figure has been affected by changes in the value of Alphabet’s investments, which include a stake in SpaceX. Elon Musk’s rocket maker fell about 4 per cent during the period, contributing to an $8.7 billion net loss on equity investments.

Operating income, which does not include investment losses, rose 30 per cent to $40.6 billion but missed Wall Street’s expectations for $43.2 billion.

Ashkenazi noted that a $5.2 billion cash payment to settle a 2018 European regulatory fine contributed to the more deeply negative cash flows. Google recently lost an appeal against a verdict that it engaged in anticompetitive behaviour via its Android operating system.

Offsetting the gloom in search, Alphabet’s cloud business doubled its sales to $30.7 billion, benefiting from surging customer demand for its own AI services as well as selling computing capacity to rivals such as start-up Anthropic.

Google has touted its “full-stack” AI strategy as a big strategic advantage, developing its own chips, data centres and frontier models, which are then delivered to billions of loyal consumers via its established apps and services.

Chief executive Sundar Pichai has been criticised for being slow to deploy AI and allowing a company of Google’s scale to fall behind start-ups such as Anthropic and OpenAI in the lucrative enterprise sector.

Pichai said two new versions of its most advanced Gemini models – Argon and Carbon – have closed the gap in coding, finance and cyber security and should help Alphabet win back market share. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>Amy Osborne<![CDATA[Up to 3,000 Irish jobs under threat as Dealz owner seeks UK court protection ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/up-to-3000-irish-jobs-under-threat-as-dealz-owner-seeks-uk-court-protection/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/up-to-3000-irish-jobs-under-threat-as-dealz-owner-seeks-uk-court-protection/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 18:28:07 +0000Up to 3,000 jobs across Ireland could be at risk after the owner of the Dealz discount store chain filed notification in the UK of its intention to appoint an administrator to the company.

The move provides protection from creditors for the business which operates about 600 stores in the UK under the Poundland brand.

Dealz, which operates more than 70 stores in Ireland, is a wholly owned subsidiary of Poundland and its position is unclear in the light of its parent’s latest troubles. A spokesman for the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment said it had not received any notification of potential redundancies as of Thursday afternoon.

Efforts to contact the London offices of the company proved unsuccessful on Thursday but reporting in the Guardian suggested the Irish chain was likely to be impacted by the move.

In addition to its stores, which are spread across the State, the company operates a big distribution centre in Clonee, Co Meath.

Poundland was founded in Burton upon Trent in 1990 operating a single price model. It opened its first two stores in Ireland in August 2011.

Growing concerns over a fiscal crisis in France have led to a widening in the spread of sovereign bond yields, fuelling speculation at times that the ECB will have to intervene to stop financial stress from spreading to other countries.

That comes as the bank prepares for a new president, chief economist and an executive board member in charge of market operations in 2027.

Faced with increasing risks to the growth and inflation outlook, the ECB needs to ensure the smooth transmission of its monetary stance and a smooth transition in leadership.

The ECB has been in similar situations before, but this time looks different regarding the inflation outlook, geopolitical context and personnel dynamics.

Energy prices remain elevated and early signs of the second-round effects of that on consumer prices are emerging. While underlying inflationary and wage pressures have remained contained for now, they have not eased either.

Candidates to replace ECB president Christine Lagarde

With the not-so-distant experience of the 2022 crisis in mind, concerns that inflation expectations may become entrenched are likely to be weighing on ECB policymakers. Unless growth slows abruptly, a hawkish bias is likely to remain the default option for now.

Meanwhile, broad financial conditions have tightened amid a rise in bond yields driven by a combination of global and domestic factors, including geopolitical tensions, the surge in AI-driven corporate borrowing, and fiscal concerns. The latest ECB bank lending survey suggests banks are already tightening lending standards, while demand for new loans is weakening.

Higher borrowing costs and tighter credit conditions should reduce the need for further increases in policy rates, all else equal, but the ECB is facing a bigger communication challenge.

On the one hand, it has the appropriate toolkit to address financial fragmentation across the euro zone member states. In particular, ECB staff must be squarely focused on the repo market, a key transmission channel of monetary policy to the real economy, ready to intervene in case of stress.

From a technical perspective, preventing a liquidity crisis is the easy part.

On the other hand, the ECB can only ensure financial stability to the extent that it does not fuel moral hazard. Buying French debt without strict conditions would be legally and politically unacceptable. Pre-emptive ECB intervention in the French bond market looks highly unlikely in advance of an uncertain high-stakes presidential election in spring 2027.

Alternatively, any hint that the bank may activate the bond-buying tool known as the transmission protection instrument (TPI) would risk making French problems worse. This tool was created in 2022 to prevent fragmentation in the euro zone bond markets, but it comes with conditions and has never been used so far. Tweaking the TPI conditionality to make France eligible may be politically toxic in other countries.

Ideally, verbal intervention would suffice. The question is whether proverbial constructive ambiguity can work in France’s case – a communication strategy the ECB has long relied on to signal willingness to intervene while preserving flexibility.

These trade-offs come at a time when heads of state and government will need to agree on a large package of nominations for the bank’s executive board in coming months.

Bank president Christine Lagarde has now announced her departure. This will allow governments to decide on all executive board replacements before the French election. The changeover will inevitably raise questions about the direction of policy under the next leadership.

France is likely heading towards ECB support and a Marine Le Pen presidency

In that context, Klaas Knot’s self-described approach of “principled pragmatism” looks particularly relevant. The former president of the Dutch central bank and a contender for the top job argued that the European Central Bank would need to keep acting decisively to preserve monetary transmission in the future without becoming a substitute for fiscal or political action.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, the former governor of the Bank of Spain, is another strong candidate with the credentials and experience to run the ECB.

Both have been in charge during previous economic and fiscal crises. Whoever gets the job will need to strike the right balance between principles and pragmatism in the next one. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>The Washington Post<![CDATA[Farewell to ‘aeroplane mode’: Flying loses its status as the last internet black hole]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/29/easyjet-internet-in-flight-wifi-starlink-elon-musk-aer-lingus-ryanair-short-haul/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/10/29/easyjet-internet-in-flight-wifi-starlink-elon-musk-aer-lingus-ryanair-short-haul/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 06:00:01 +0000Back in 1997, an episode of Seinfeld introduced the world to a unique approach to long-haul travel. David Puddy, played by Patrick Warburton, the boyfriend of Elaine Benes (Julia Louis Dreyfus), decided he would just stare at the back of the seat in front of him for the whole flight.

No television, no movies, no headphones, no books, not even a nap. He was going to sit upright, eyes-open, and stare straight ahead for what was meant to be a very long trip.

Although this was wild even to contemplate almost three decades ago, it isn’t viewed in quite so simple a light today.

Is airplane mode really just a setting on your phone? That’s the philosophical question that has moved to the foreground in recent days.

On Monday, EasyJet announced it would install Elon Musk’s Starlink internet across its fleet during the first half of next year, with roll-out completed in 2028.

Aer Lingus already offers Starlink on its transatlantic flights with plans eventually to extend it to European flights.

The jump from wifi of any standard on a plane being impressive to high speed being the norm has come about rather quickly.

Aer Lingus has begun its free in-flight wifi. Bang goes a rare oasis of tranquillity

Airline wifi has, for most of the 20 years it has been available, been somewhat of a joke. Typically it has been considered slow, expensive and definitely not reliable. Yet that’s far too broad an assumption.

Even back in 2019, I recall an Air France trip back from China where I was overjoyed that the quality was good enough to watch Dublin beat Mayo in the All Ireland semi-final. Still, that was definitely the exception, not the norm.

With Starlink’s satellites orbiting around 550 kilometres above ground, they are shortening the journey that was previously needed for signals to reach planes.

With the Aer Lingus transatlantic fleet as an example, the speeds promised exceed 500Mbps. When it comes to connectivity quality, that’s absolutely stellar stuff.

With EasyJet, well it’s essentially the same service only focused squarely on short-haul. That is rather new as plane wifi has thus far almost exclusively been targeted at long-haul by carriers in Europe.

It is a huge step for wifi to go from being an available extra service towards it being expected on all journeys in the not-too-distant future. It’s heavenly to some of you and no doubt a nightmare to others.

That’s because the last acceptable excuse for being unreachable is disappearing. An aeroplane is one of the few places where you have outright immunity from checking emails or messages. That’s from everyone in your life, although, for most of us, the first thing to come to mind is work.

“I’m 35,000 feet above ground embracing the engineering miracle of mechanised flight” won’t necessarily be considered a good enough excuse any more.

Yet the benefits are substantial. That game I watched back in 2019 was exactly what I needed. I’d just spent a couple of hours in Hong Kong airport interviewing protesters and it was emotionally moving and draining. Being able to decompress by watching Con O’Callaghan and Paul Mannion run riot was the best possible thing for me at the time.

There’s also the matter of parents travelling with children. As a child-free person, I was surprised by how popular YouTube premium is with parents. Several have told me it’s the last subscription they would consider giving up. For them it is a reliable way to make sure their kids have access to their favourite videos while travelling. Getting that access on planes only adds to that support for parents.

Connectivity doesn’t have to be about productivity. An employer who expects you to stay connected with work when you’re on a plane probably has a lot more wrong with them than just that.

Smart bosses know that rest matters. Even remotely intelligent ones know that flights are tiring in and of themselves, so it’s not like you’re getting a net productivity benefit by irking staff while they’re strapped to a seat high above the ground.

Retaining the ability to disconnect should not come down to whether there actually is a connection.

Not everyone agrees with the move to connect and that includes airlines. For the foreseeable future, Ryanair is not going to embrace Starlink.

Michael O’Leary has said plainly that he felt the cost/benefit analysis just did not compute for his airline.

Still, where it is an option, it’s important that people remember that an option means they have a choice.

Warburton has jokingly apologised for his character kicking off the unfortunately named “rawdogging” trend. This, however, is not a choice of extremes. Those who feel the need to stare at the back of a chair still can, while, in the near future, those who want optimal connectivity will have it.

Everything in between is also on the table and a matter of free will. You can just watch a movie on the screen, follow the map or listen to something downloaded on your phone. You’ll simply have more choices as to what you can do.

If your concern is not being able to disconnect, then you really shouldn’t blame the airline. Instead, ask who or what in your work or personal life makes you feel the need to be always on. Then address that deeper issue, which is beyond Aer Lingus’ or EasyJet’s pay grade.

Increasingly, organisations are offering employee benefits such as financial assistance with fertility treatment and egg freezing but, culturally and behaviourally, they are lagging behind in supporting workers who choose these options, according to researchers at DCU’s Institute for Business and Society.

Pregnancy and parenthood can be a time of great joy and anticipation but for those having trouble conceiving – or those who have miscarried – it can be filled with anxiety, fear and even shame.

Organisational behaviour specialist Céire Gilsenan experienced all these emotions and more when she was going through her first fertility journey while working full-time. She kept the circle of trust small so, besides her partner, only her sister knew she was undergoing IVF.

At work, she slipped out surreptitiously for doctor’s appointments and for phone calls about her results.

“I remember distinctly sitting in the clinic, just feeling so uncomfortable and pretending to read the paper because I was terrified of seeing somebody that I knew. I was physically sweating because I knew I was going to be late back to work, and you’re trying to think of an excuse of where you were.”

Gilsenan felt extremely vulnerable as her high-pressure workplace clashed with the demands of intensive medical protocols. Her experience is not that unusual, according to researchers.

“Work and motherhood are never more on a collision than they are during fertility treatment,” says Prof Yseult Freeney of DCU, who studies women in the workplace. “Fertility treatment is like a second job. It’s a second shift, but it’s one that they can’t control because they don’t know when it’s going to happen. They also really can’t control when they’re going to get bad news.”

Fertility treatment and the workplace: ‘It’s a hugely personal thing to have to say’

For partners, Freeney says, they’re often “meant to be the strong person in this, but the challenges for them are equally hard, just different. They’re not as physical but they’re absolutely as emotional.”

A VHI survey, Fertility in Focus: The Workplace Realities, found that 14 per cent of women surveyed in 2024 had experienced fertility issues. Of those, two-thirds said it had interfered with work, while only 20 per cent felt prepared and 64 per cent feared future health problems if their stress continued.

Of the respondents, only 27 per cent had spoken to their employer and 74 per cent had sought advice from their GP.

Gilsenan’s decision not to reveal her situation to her colleagues or wider family was deliberate. “I felt that if it didn’t go well, I wouldn’t be able to deal with my own distress and handle other people’s distress or reaction to my distress.”

Her fertility journey was ultimately successful. Afterwards she decided to research this emerging area further. She was the lead author on Experiencing and Responding to Existential Vulnerability: Navigating the Work–Fertility Treatment Interface, published in the Gender, Work and Organisation Journal. Gilsenan was supervised by Freeney and assisted by fellow researchers Lisa van der Werff and Hilary O’Leary of DCU’s Institute for Business and Society.

Gilsenan interviewed 18 other women who had undergone fertility treatment while working full-time. “People had miscarriages and went back to work the next day. They got phone calls at work to say that the treatment hadn’t worked for the third or fourth time and just went back out of that meeting room and into the office like everything was normal.”

Although fertility treatment was gruelling physically and emotionally, all felt it was important to maintain a professional identity. Their desire to work, and be recognised at work, did not pause just because they were trying to become parents.

Whether or not the woman chose to reveal her fertility treatment to family or colleagues, the research found that feelings of vulnerability were common, and the women navigated the work-fertility interface in three distinct ways: masking, confronting and succumbing.

  • Masking is the exhausting, active pretence of hiding your physical and emotional distress to protect a professional image. This was the most common response and included hiding appointments, overworking, crying in the toilet and then presenting a brave face in public. Freeney says there’s a feeling among the women that “they can’t put all their eggs in one basket. So, ‘If this is not going to work out, I have to have something else to fall back on’. They then overinvest in work by adopting a masking response.”
  • Confronting is when the woman decides to tell a trusted manager or colleague and reclaim some control over her life and time. This helps them set shared boundaries and expectations around appointments and calls. For example, Gilsenan revealed the situation to a concerned colleague, and this provided great relief. “She would cover for me and she even came to the clinic with me a few times. It genuinely did make a world of difference.”
  • Succumbing is when the hopeful parent reaches a point of being overwhelmed and can no longer manage their vulnerability, says Freeney. Their capacity to cope has been exceeded and they might start stepping back from projects and feel a profound loss of hope.

One interviewee recounted her first performance review after treatment ended. She told her manager: “Stop talking to me about performance. I don’t care about it any more. I have no one to put through college.”

The paper finds that telling a manager, member of HR or a colleague doesn’t end the vulnerability or distress, and many keep masking even after telling someone.

Gilsenan said of the medical process: “I’ll inject myself a million times. I’ll go through those awful tests and procedures. It didn’t take a jot out of me.” The hard part, she says, was the “anguish of the whole thing, the uncertainty, how vulnerable you are, how unpredictable it is”.

Workplace wellbeing and productivity go hand in hand, so offering to pay for fertility benefits isn’t enough on its own. Organisations should foster compassionate, informed workplace cultures that support employee wellbeing, engagement and retention while reducing the stigma often associated with fertility challenges.

The DCU researchers hope that by making this hidden dimension of working life visible, organisations will build cultures that reduce the weight of existential vulnerability for aspiring parents.

‘Injecting yourself daily is difficult to navigate at work’: Managing fertility treatment while working

Creating fertility-aware workplaces doesn’t mean having all the answers. “You don’t need a policy to lead with empathy and compassion,” says Gilsenan.

Often, the most meaningful support begins with awareness and flexibility for those undergoing treatment. Women shouldn’t have to make up lies to cover appointments, says Freeney. The work is getting done; they just need some flexibility.

“Employees who feel supported by their employer during significant life experiences are more likely to remain engaged, loyal and connected to their organisation. In contrast, employees who feel they must hide their fertility journey may experience increased stress, absenteeism, disengagement and isolation,” says the Sims IVF clinic.

VHI recommends stress supports and counselling, fertility education talks, including fertility in wellness programmes, and flexible working and leave.

]]>Colin Keegan<![CDATA[A 97-year-old woman faces €455,000 payment to Bank of Ireland over life loan taken out in 2003]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/life-loan-proves-a-millstone-for-97-year-old-pensioner/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/life-loan-proves-a-millstone-for-97-year-old-pensioner/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000I would like to draw your attention to a very serious issue involving a Bank of Ireland life loan to an elderly lady. I am hoping that by having this case highlighted it will help speed up our efforts to have the issue resolved, and also serve as a cautionary tale to anyone else considering taking on a life loan.

Back in 2003, when she was 72, a single woman with no children received correspondence from Bank of Ireland offering her a life loan. Having taken legal advice (she never discussed this advice with anyone), she took out a life loan of €130,000.

She actually only needed €30,000 at the time, so she put €100,000 back on deposit with Bank of Ireland, where it has remained ever since. (It is not clear why she took out €130,000 when she only needed €30,000.)

As of June this year, the total amount required to close the account was a staggering €455,081. The woman is now 97.

Her nieces and nephews have been trying unsuccessfully to get mediation on this loan with Bank of Ireland since 2022. A complaint was made in August last year to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO), but in a response in May this year, the ombudsman said it could be another 12-14 months before we hear from them on this complaint.

The general public needs to be more aware of the risks involved in life loans. While Bank of Ireland no longer offer such a product, there are ads for similar products from Spry Finance frequently aired on radio.

The behaviour of Bank of Ireland at all stages of this loan needs to be questioned and answers given.

The fact that the FSPO can tell a 97-year-old that it will be 12 to 14 months before a member of the investigative team will be appointed to this case is shocking.

JC

Any regular reader will know that while I accept life loans and similar equity release products can be useful for certain borrowers, my view is that they are very much credit of last resource – something you turn to only if you cannot raise money you need any other way.

They were, as you say, popular in the early years of this century and heavily marketed by the lenders offering them, including Bank of Ireland. They offered people who might be wealthy on paper due to the value of their home but cash poor – especially women with little or no pension cover – access to money that would not need to be repaid in their lifetime.

Lifeline or life sentence? How equity-release lifetime loans work

Interest built up over time and the loan was redeemed when you died or otherwise moved out of or sold the property. That interest could, and in some cases did, swallow up all the equity in a home. However, where the debt was greater than the eventual sale price, the bank committed not to chase the estate for any payment over and above the sale price.

The collapse of property prices saw them swiftly withdrawn from the market, alongside tracker loans, as banks faced the prospect of losing money on both products.

Your friend’s story is almost a textbook case study of what can go wrong.

Life loans were available only to those over the age of 65. People could borrow up to 20 per cent of the value of their homes if they were in their 60s to as much as 30 per cent for those in their 80s. For someone like your friend, borrowing at 72, the limit was 25 per cent.

The first alarm is that, as you tell it, she never proactively sought this loan; instead, she was simply targeted with marketing material by the bank.

What are your options if you want to release wealth tied up in your home?

This was certainly not unusual back in the wild west of the early noughties in the credit markets. People regularly got letters at that time telling them they had been pre-approved for loans they had never sought and found their credit card borrowing limits had been increased without any contact from or with them.

Was any of this ethical, including love-bombing a pensioner with offers of “easy-to-access” money? In my view, certainly not.

Does it amount to mis-selling? I’m certainly not going to second-guess the ombudsman when it comes to that. The FSPO is an office with far more resources and expertise than me, as well as long experience with such cases and clear lines of communication with the very top echelons of lenders such as Bank of Ireland.

But there are features of your friend’s story that are deeply concerning. While the woman was obliged under the terms of the loan to consult a solicitor – who had to sign forms to confirm their engagement – the bank also had a duty of care to ensure that it was selling appropriate products to people.

The fact that €100,000 of this €130,000 borrowed never moved from the deposit account into which it was lodged at Bank of Ireland should have raised alarm bells with the bank.

Bank of Ireland notes that, as in this case, it could be decades before repayment fell due. Interest on your friend’s loan has been building up for 25 years.

Equity release borrowing by older homeowners jumps 30% to €75m

“To ensure customers would understand the product, the information provided clearly explained the terms of the loan,” a spokesman for Bank of Ireland says. And, having read the product brochure, those terms should be very clear to anyone who took the time to read it in full. It is not hidden in seven-point type.

“Most importantly,” the bank continues, “before any life loan was agreed it was a requirement for each customer to obtain independent legal advice – and to show that they had taken that legal advice – to ensure that customers fully understood the terms and conditions.”

Whatever about Bank of Ireland mis-selling this loan, there are questions about the advice any legal practitioner gave this woman back in 2003. She clearly did not “need” this money – or most of it anyway – as €100,000 has sat untouched on deposit ever since, effectively losing value. It is just such a bad call on so many levels.

So what “advice” the solicitor provided, I have no idea. I can see them saying they advised only on the legal and contractual issues rather than the wisdom of taking the loan but that seems a very narrow and unhelpful interpretation of their role.

Reader’s attempts to foil fraudsters hit weird Bank of Ireland roadblock

The bank certainly appears to be sticking to its view that the loan has worked exactly as it should and as it was advised to the client. Whether that passes muster with the ombudsman remains to be seen, especially given she borrowed money under this expensive product that she clearly did not need. How was that assessed?

As for the ombudsman, I have sympathy. Asking a 97-year-old to hold on for up to 14 months to hear if they have a case certainly seems insensitive but the resources of the ombudsman are limited and all the cases that get to the investigation stage have people who are feeling hard done by, so how can they prioritise other than first come, first served.

It is simply unfortunate that it took so long for the details of this loan to emerge so that her extended family could help her.

First and foremost, it highlights the extent to which the public system is the loser in the incestuous relationship between public hospitals and private medicine, which has developed over the years, allowing publicly employed consultants to see private patients in public hospitals and avail of facilities funded by the State.

It has proved lucrative for the medical profession, which is not without influence. Thus the arrangement is very hard to dismantle – as demonstrated by the recent row over public consultants continuing to carry out private work in Dublin’s Rotunda Hospital. Somehow, this privilege has come to be seen as a sort of birthright for aspiring Irish consultant doctors.

The fact that this practice continues at Irish hospitals is hard enough to understand, but the idea that the hospitals in question are not billing the health insurance companies that make the whole thing supposedly viable is beyond comprehension.

The precise reason for public hospitals’ failure to collect the €125 million they are owed has not been elucidated. But the public accounts committee says that, according to the HSE, the number one reason is: “Consultants not completing the claim form on a timely basis, and [the] insurer refuses to process the claim as it has exceeded their allowable time for claim submission.”

According to Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill, no one in particular is to blame. “The consultant has to make sure to sign it [the claim] within a year. It has to be processed by the hospital and the HSE, and the insurance company has to pay it,” she has said.

Consultants’ private healthcare in public settings has ‘ceased’, HSE review finds

The health service is not noted for its efficiency, but when the minister of the day is reduced to asking people who work for her – consultants and others – to please do their job out of some sort of sense of duty or personal responsibility, you really have to wonder what is going on.

It’s unclear how much, if any, of the €125 million relates to VHI, but a failure to pay public hospitals on its part would be unsporting, to put it mildly

It is very hard to imagine the boss of a private sector company not wanting to apportion responsibility for a failure to collect €125 million, and instead just asking everybody involved to try a little harder in future.

The private health insurers are not exactly blameless either. Health insurance is big business in Ireland. Almost one in every two people has a policy, which is well above European norms. In Europe, the model tends towards State funding or mandatory public health insurance. In many ways, the Irish private health insurance industry is the yin to the yang of the tradition of allowing private medicine to be carried out in public hospitals.

Rotunda Hospital’s clash with Coalition over private maternity care deepens

The largest player in the market, with an almost 50 per cent share of it, is the VHI, which is owned by the State. It’s unclear how much, if any, of the €125 million relates to VHI, but a failure to pay public hospitals on its part would be unsporting, to put it mildly. ]]><![CDATA[Pension or the new investment account: where should your spare cash go?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/28/pension-or-the-new-investment-account-where-should-your-spare-cash-go/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/28/pension-or-the-new-investment-account-where-should-your-spare-cash-go/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Do you have spare cash sitting on deposit? If so, there’s a strong case for taking advantage of generous pension tax relief. But with a new Government-backed personal investment account set to open next July, are your spare savings better off going there instead?

Irish households had a whopping €175 billion sitting in low-interest bank accounts in the first six months of 2026, says the Central Bank. By leaving more than you need on deposit below the rate of inflation, the value of your money is shrinking. There are definitely better things to do with it.

Putting your spare cash towards an additional voluntary contribution (AVC) to your pension or into the new personal investment account (PIA) are both good ideas. But, before you move a cent, which is best for you?

Pension play

An AVC lets you add extra funds to your pension, topping up the regular contributions you and your employer make. Not only is this boosting your retirement savings, but you’ll get significant tax relief too.

“AVCs are among the most powerful, yet underutilised ways for Irish employees to build personal wealth,” says Niall O’Connor, founder of Financial Planning Matters.

The tax relief is most generous for higher earners. A single person earning €44,000 a year or more will benefit from 40 per cent tax relief on contributions.

Put €100 into your pension, for example, and the full €100 goes into your pot, where it can grow and compound tax-free, and the Government will give you €40 back. So, your €100 contribution costs you just €60.

Lower rate taxpayers get 20 per cent tax relief on contributions.

“You can effectively turn €6,000 of your own money into €10,000 invested towards retirement,” says O’Connor of higher rate taxpayers.

“This is a considerable advantage, before the investment has earned a single cent.”

It’s important to understand the age-related pension contribution limits within which you qualify for the tax relief.

If you’re aged 30 to 39, for example, you can contribute up to 20 per cent of your income and be eligible for the tax relief. This rises to 25 per cent for those aged 40 to 49, 30 per cent for those aged 50-54, jumping to 35 per cent for those aged up to 59 and 40 per cent for those aged over 60.

This is based on eligible earnings up to a ceiling of €115,000.

Importantly, the limits include your existing pension contributions. Take the example of a 40-year-old on €80,000 who already contributes 6 per cent of their salary to pension.

“The maximum personal contribution qualifying for tax relief would be €20,000,” says O’Connor. “Having already contributed €4,800, they could make an AVC of up to €15,200.”

They could contribute more, but they won’t get tax relief on anything over the 25 per cent limit for their age.

As a higher rate 40 per cent taxpayer, they make a tax saving at 40 per cent on their contribution so that €15,200 going into their pension only costs them €9,120. Revenue will give them a refund of €6,080, says O’Connor.

The upfront tax refund on an AVC is hard to beat, and your money can also benefit from tax-free investment growth within the pension as your money compounds in the years ahead.

If that €15,200 AVC remained invested over 25 years, assuming a 5 per cent annual investment return after charges, it could grow to approximately €51,500, says O’Connor.

Similarly, for someone aged 50 earning €100,000 who is already contributing 8 per cent of salary to their pension, their remaining personal contribution limit qualifying for relief would be 22 per cent of their salary, or €22,000.

After tax relief, contributing €22,000 to their pension only costs them €13,200.

Pension investments can go up or down of course but invested for 15 years at an illustrative 5 per cent annual return after charges, that single €22,000 contribution could grow to approximately €45,700, says O’Connor.

Money saved in a deposit account comes from your after-tax income, meaning you’ve already paid tax on those earnings and receive no additional tax relief for saving them, says Nick Charalambous, managing director of Alpha Wealth.

Keep €10,000 on deposit earning 2 per cent interest and it would generate just €134 a year once 33 per cent deposit interest tax is deducted.

With inflation running at 4 per cent, the cost of living is rising faster than the interest you are earning, so savings are actually losing purchasing power, says Charalambous.

“Watching your bank balance grow doesn’t necessarily mean you are building wealth.”

Having some accessible savings is essential of course. Don’t put your emergency fund or money for short-term goals into your pension.

“It makes little financial sense if you subsequently find yourself having to borrow at 7 or 8 per cent to fund another financial priority,” he says.

Personal investment account

Think of the Government’s new personal investment account as complementary to pension saving, not a replacement for it, says Charalambous.

Due to launch next July, you will be able to put up to €12,000 a year into the account, with a 1 per cent tax kicking in on any amount above the €50,000 tax-free threshold.

Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work

Lodge the full €12,000 and, unlike a pension contribution, you will not get anything back now from Revenue by way of tax relief. Any gains will, however, be able to grow without capital gains tax, exit tax or dividend withholding tax.

How much could your money grow? As with a pension, there are no guarantees. The S&P 500, which tracks the top 500 listed US companies, has returned about 6-8 per cent on an inflation-adjusted basis every year over the past 20 years.

There have been periods of downturn, however, so if you need to cash in your investment when markets are down, you do face the risk of losing your money.

Both pension and the PIA can offer tax-efficient investment growth, says O’Connor, but the mechanisms differ.

Pension funds generally benefit from tax-free investment growth while your money remains within the pension, with taxes applied when benefits are taken.

Under the proposed PIA, there is no tax on investments under the €50,000 threshold but a 1 per cent annual charge would apply on any amount over that.

This could mean paying tax on the account in years when your investment is losing money, simply because the overall balance exceeds €50,000.

“For somebody paying 40 per cent income tax, with sufficient unused pension contribution capacity and money genuinely intended for retirement, I would generally examine the AVC opportunity first because of the immediate tax relief available,” says O’Connor.

But once you’ve got your pension on track, the PIA could provide an attractive additional vehicle for accumulating wealth outside the pension system, he says.

Taxing times

Getting 40 per cent tax relief on pension contributions on the way in is great, but won’t I pay tax at 40 per cent when I take the money in retirement? Financial advisers get asked this all the time, says O’Connor.

It’s possible to get the 40 per cent income tax relief on your pension contribution and draw income from the pot in retirement without paying tax at the 40 per cent rate, says O’Connor.

Under current rules, you can generally draw down a quarter of your fund at retirement as a tax-free lump sum. The first €200,000 of qualifying retirement lump sums received over an individual’s lifetime is free of income tax. The next €300,000 is generally taxed at 20 per cent, he says.

The income tax rate you pay after that depends on how much you draw down from your fund each year.

Take a single retiree aged 66 who has €500,000 invested in an approved retirement fund (ARF) and is getting the maximum State pension, equivalent to about €15,564 a year.

If they withdraw 4 per cent of the ARF annually, or €20,000, this gives them a total retirement income of €35,564. That is below the €44,000 threshold this year for higher-rate income tax, says O’Connor. That threshold rises next year to €46,500.

Even someone with a €700,000 ARF who is withdrawing 4 per cent annually, or €28,000 a year when combined with the State pension, would have approximately €43,564 a year, still below the threshold for higher income tax.

These figures do assume the person has no other sources of taxable retirement income, such as a separate defined benefit or foreign pension, rental income or other investment withdrawals, he says.

Biggest difference to your pension pot is not how much money you put in

Accessibility

Another big difference when choosing between the AVC and the PIA for spare cash is accessibility, says Charalambous.

“The PIA’s main attraction is greater flexibility, allowing people to invest for medium- to long-term goals, without having to wait until retirement to access their money,” he says.

This will make it more attractive to those wanting to accumulate wealth for things other than retirement.

The fact that an investment receives favourable tax treatment does not automatically make it right for you.

“I would never recommend transferring all available cash into a pension simply to generate a tax refund,” says O’Connor.

How big should your pension pot be for a comfortable retirement in Ireland?

Before deciding what to do, identify three categories of money, he says: what you need available in the short term; what should be invested for medium- and long-term objectives; and what can be committed to retirement.

The PIA may become an attractive option for the second category, while AVCs can be particularly powerful for the third.

I need help tracking down a lost pension from my first job nearly 50 years ago

Use it or lose it

If you do have spare cash and you haven’t yet maxed out your pension contributions, don’t wait for the PIA to launch before acting, says Charalambous.

Pension tax relief is linked to the year – so use it or lose it.

“The mistake is missing an opportunity to claim valuable pension tax relief now while waiting for a scheme that hasn’t launched yet,” he says.

To claim tax relief against your earnings for last year (2025), an AVC must be made by October 31st of the current year.

There is an extended deadline of November 18th for Revenue Online Service (ROS) users such as those self-employed or tax agents handling self-assessed income tax.

“I would strongly encourage people to review their pension before the tax deadline. The tax advantages are simply too valuable to overlook,” says Charalambous.

You’ll need to act fast to claim pension relief against your 2025 earnings.

To make an AVC, first check how much unused personal pension contribution capacity remains for 2025, says O’Connor. Payroll or your pension provider should be able to tell you this.

Call Revenue and ask about your actual income tax position for 2025. Not everyone will qualify for 40 per cent tax relief on every euro contributed, even if they are generally considered a higher-rate taxpayer, he says.

Third, confirm you have sufficient cash to fund the contribution in the short term before any refund is received.

Fourth, think about how you want the pension AVC to be invested – in the same way as your payroll contributions or differently?

Making the contribution involves filling out a form, available through your pension provider’s website and a clearly labelled bank transfer to your pension provider’s account number on the form.

Pensions: In pursuit of financial security ... although chilly reality awaits

Choice

Any Government initiative to encourage Irish people to invest more rather than to continue stockpiling cash on deposit is a good thing but think of AVCs and PIAs as apples and oranges. They serve two different purposes.

But provided you have enough accessible funds to serve your short-term needs, either option is preferable to holding your wealth in cash deposits, says O’Connor.

For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account.

“But for someone who has already maximised their pension contributions, or who wants to build investments they can access before retirement, it could be an attractive addition to their financial plan,” says Charalambous.

]]>Pavel Herasimau

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, has sparked controversy by appearing to suggest that Poland and some other allied European Union member states could launch the process of leaving the EU if they fail in efforts to reform it.

His remarks were condemned by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and other figures from the pro-EU ruling coalition, who have long accused Kaczyński and his national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party of seeking “Polexit” from the EU.

However, Kaczyński responded by accusing Tusk of misrepresenting his words, insisting that he wants Poland to reform the EU rather than leave it.

Kaczyński pomylił Krynicę z Kremlem. pic.twitter.com/tX0G04krze

— Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) October 29, 2026

The comments in question came in an hour-long speech by Kaczyński at the Krynica Forum, an annual conference bringing together leaders from politics, business and civil society, which he used to outline his vision for sweeping reforms of the EU.

Repeating his longstanding criticism of Brussels, Kaczyński warned that there had been a “consistent drive to transform the EU into a centralised state” with too much power over national governments. He also called the European Parliament in its current form a “parody”.

But soon, said Kaczyński, “a window of opportunity” for reform may appear because “completely different governments could emerge” in Poland, France and Spain, all of which will hold elections within the year.

PiS has previously enjoyed close relations with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN) party in France and the nationalist Vox party of Santiago Abascal in Spain.

The EU is preparing a "German plan" that would "annihilate the Polish state", said Kaczyński as Poland marks Independence Day.

He warned that the incoming opposition government will "strive to implement this plan" and called on Poles to "fight" against it https://t.co/QDbxmiaazJ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2023

Kaczyński suggested that Poland, if led by PiS, could work with other like-minded EU governments to push for reform of the bloc by influencing public opinion, identifying breaches of EU treaties, creating a blocking minority in the European Council, and trying to change the EU’s treaties.

However, the PiS leader then warned that, “if [those] approaches fail to yield results, the states that want change could conclude a new treaty with the elements we are seeking, but with a delayed entry into force”.

Kaczyński then noted that the EU treaties “include provisions specifying the terms under which a state may withdraw from the EU. This all begins with negotiations. And simply begin these negotiations”.

“It is a tough approach, a risky one, but the situation is so dire that it is worth employing such a method if all others fail to yield results,” he added.

 

The remarks immediately prompted condemnation from figures in Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused Kaczyński of effectively calling for Polexit – something they have long claimed he wants, even though PiS has not explicitly called for it before.

“Jarosław Kaczyński has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the terms of its withdrawal from the EU,” wrote Tusk himself on X. “This is, among other things, what the current struggle in Poland is about – a tough struggle. I do not intend to lose it.”

“So they do want Polexit after all,” wrote foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Customs borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania…An end to subsidies for farmers and investments…And they swore on their lives that they’d never do that.”

In a video published later on Thursday, Tusk declared that next year’s parliamentary elections would help decide “whether Poland remains in the European Union or leaves it”.

Jarosław Kaczyński ogłosił właśnie, że Polska powinna zacząć rokowania o warunkach wyjścia z Unii Europejskiej. O taką między innymi stawkę toczy się dziś w Polsce walka. Twarda walka. Nie zamierzam jej przegrać, nawet jeśli nie wszyscy zagrają ze mną.

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 29, 2026

Kaczyński responded by saying that “Tusk is lying as usual”. He emphasised that he believes “the EU is needed but it requires thorough reform” so that it “benefits not the elites, but ordinary citizens”.

PiS deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek said on Thursday that his party was “considering all scenarios, including the possibility that the EU will kill itself”. However, he added that the priority remained reforming the bloc and “PiS has no plans to leave the EU”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

When PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it regularly clashed with Brussels over a variety of issues, including judicial reform, trade, climate policy, and migration. Since Tusk, a former president of the European Council, took power in 2023, his government has greatly improved relations with Brussels.

Tusk jak zwykle kłamie. Najwyraźniej wychodzi z założenia, że dzień bez kłamstwa jest dniem straconym…

Unia Europejska jest potrzebna, ale wymaga gruntownej reformy. Kryzys i zapaść w jej obecnym kształcie to efekt rządów Merkel i jednego z jej pomocników, Tuska. Nie ma co się…

— Jarosław Kaczyński (@OficjalnyJK) October 29, 2026

Poland has been the largest net recipient of EU funding since joining the bloc in 2004. A study published earlier this year found that the country’s economy is 42% larger than it would have been had Poland not been part of the EU.

Opinion polls consistently show a large majority of Poles in favour of remaining part of the EU. However, recent years have seen an uptick in support for Polexit, as well as for anti-EU far-right parties.

Regular polling by state research agency CBOS shows that, while opposition to EU membership fell to a record low of 5% in 2022, it has subsequently risen and stood at 14% in the most recent survey.

]]> Polish bishop convicted for failing to promptly report child sex abuse allegations https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/29/polish-bishop-convicted-for-failing-to-promptly-report-child-sex-abuse-allegations/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 13:45:01 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106178

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

In the first ruling of its kind in Poland, a Catholic bishop has been found guilty of failing to promptly inform the law enforcement authorities about allegations of child sex abuse committed by priests under his authority.

Andrzej Jeż, the bishop of Tarnów, was handed a non-custodial sentence that will require him to donate 25% of his earnings for two years to a charity that supports victims of child sexual abuse.

However, the verdict can still be appealed, and the diocese of Tarnów has already announced that it “disagrees with the court’s ruling” and that an appeal will be filed.

Pierwszy taki wyrok w Polsce. Biskup skazany za zwlekanie z powiadomieniem prokuratury o pedofilach w sutannach

Ordynariusz tarnowski bp Andrzej Jeż jest pierwszym biskupem oskarżonym o zbyt późne powiadomienie prokuratury o pedofilii w Kościele. I pierwszym, który który został…

— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 29, 2026

The case relates to alleged abuse by two priests who worked under Jeż’s authority. They can be identified only as Stanisław P. and Tomasz K. under Polish privacy law.

In 2022, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into allegations against Stanisław P. because the statute of limitations had expired, despite concluding that he had harmed at least 95 children and committed “sexual acts” against 77 of them over several decades in parishes in Poland and Ukraine.

In 2023, prosecutors decided to charge Tomasz K., who allegedly sexually abused children as early as 2018. However, they have been unable to formally present the charges to him because of his poor health, news website OKO.press reported earlier this year.

 

Though Jeż was not accused of complicity in the alleged abuse itself, he was charged under a 2017 law making it a criminal offence not to “immediately notify the authorities” of “credible information” about sexual abuse of minors. The offence is punishable by up to three years in prison.

Investigators say that, although an internal church probe into Stanisław P. was initiated in the 2000s and a decision to remove him from the clergy was made in 2013, Jeż only notified the prosecutor’s office in 2020. In the case of Tomasz K., the bishop notified prosecutors only in 2021.

In court, prosecutor Marcin Stępień said that Jeż’s failure to report the abuse promptly had allowed the statute of limitations to expire in the case of some of Stanisław P.’s victims.

Stępień also noted that the bishop had only come forward with the information when media coverage brought the allegations against Stanisław P. to light, reports broadcaster TVN.

A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers.

It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026

Prosecutors sought a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for three years, and a fine of 20,000 zloty (€4,550). Jeż, however, denied the allegations against him and sought an acquittal. He argued that he had reported the alleged abuse to the authorities as soon as there was credible information.

On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good.

In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance.

In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”.

The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up.

The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”.

In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy.

]]> Turkish engineer creates live 3D pixel map of adopted hometown Warsaw https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/28/turkish-engineer-creates-live-3d-pixel-map-of-adopted-hometown-warsaw/ Wed, 28 Oct 2026 21:36:45 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106153

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.

The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.

The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.

While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.

Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.

The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.

 

The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.

Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.

Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.

An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public.

Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2025

The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards.

The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves.

A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium.

I turned Warsaw into a flight sim 🛩️

Take off from Chopin, fly through the ring over the Palace of Culture, then land a UFO inside Stadion Narodowy as the roof opens 🛸

Desktop only for now. Can you land it? 👇 pic.twitter.com/DT2fdk1Vem

— Bedirhan (@bedcodes) October 27, 2026

Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025.

Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula.

The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”.

Poland has detained a Ukrainian citizen who is wanted by Romania on suspicion of involvement in an arson attack on a defence company carried out on behalf of Russia.

On Tuesday, the Polish police’s Central Investigation Bureau (CBŚP) announced that anti-terrorism officers had detained the man, who can be named only as Artem S. under Polish privacy law, in Warsaw under a European Arrest Warrant issued by Romania.

In the early hours of 14 September, a fire broke out in the city of Brașov, Romania, in the immediate vicinity of premises belonging to Carfil, a manufacturer of military equipment. Carfil is a subsidiary of ROMARM, a state-owned defence company.

On Monday this week, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said it had determined that the fire had been deliberately caused by a “sabotage network coordinated from Russia”. It added that “several citizens of former Soviet states who reside in the EU” had been involved in the arson attack.

The SRI also revealed that the group’s activities were not limited to Romania. “Its coordinators in Russia had assigned it a wide range of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as sites of military and industrial interest.”

 

In a separate statement, Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) confirmed that the suspects were a Ukrainian, who was at large in Poland, and two Belarusians, who had already been detained in Germany, where they “had been preparing to commit similar acts”.

Polish broadcaster RMF reports, based on sources, that Artem S.’s role in the Brașov attack was to identify a target and to arrange payment for those involved. A Polish court will now decide whether the 25-year-old should be extradited to Romania.

Poland itself has been a primary target for Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” in Europe. Many of those detained and convicted have been Ukrainian and Belarusians, though some Polish citizens have also been implicated.

“Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.”

The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan.

Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development.

“Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”.

In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place.

Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”.

 

Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland.

The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time.

Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA).

The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group.

Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019

The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”.

It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment.

On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware.

Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history.

Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026

Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”.

“The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added.

Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027.

Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline.

Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026

The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion.

But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”.

Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.

Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies

Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr

In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour.

Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20.
