Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week.

The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.

🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026

In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health.

In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases.

 

A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion.

The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%).

The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority).

One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand.

In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023

The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”.

Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”.

Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026

In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition.

However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law.

By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here)

Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now.

No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September.

He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government.

The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border.

However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024

Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision.

The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy.

Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week.

The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland.

 

Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out.

Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves.

Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”.

Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII.

On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024

This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions.

In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning.

Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago.

Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022

Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland.

If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation.

This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands.

Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute.

Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims

It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026

Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken.

As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful.

But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance.

“Power is somehow cheap now,” says Stefano Cossalter, product line director for the Lamborghini Urus. “Our number-one priority was driving dynamics. That’s the core of the Performante: suspension, brakes and calibration software.”

Not that Lamborghini’s latest ‘super-SUV’ is either underpowered or inexpensive, you understand. Its twin-turbocharged V8 and hybrid system dish up a combined 812hp and 738lb ft of torque. And the entry cost of £226,680 is almost £20,000 more than a regular 800hp Urus SE.

Worth it? That’s what I’m at Vairano, an automotive proving ground near Milan, to find out. Used regularly by Lamborghini engineers, its facilities include a skidpan, handling course and tightly coiled, two-lane circuit that resembles the best B-road you’ve ever driven. If anywhere can put the Performante’s dynamic chops to the test, it’s here. 

A brief history of Performante

‘Performante’ has become one of Sant’Agata’s most revered suffixes – second only to ‘Super Veloce’, perhaps. It first appeared on the 2017 Huracan Performante, a car that developed just 30hp more than a standard Huracan LP610-4, yet took 36 fewer seconds to circumnavigate the 12.9 miles and 73 corners of the Nurburgring. Indeed, the hardcore Huracan’s lap time of 6min 52.01sec was an outright production car record until the Porsche 911 GT2 RS shaved off another few seconds.

The first generation Urus Performante followed in 2022. With 666 devilish horsepower, an Akrapovic exhaust system, a wider track and optional Pirelli Trofeo R tyres, it undoubtedly met the brief for heightened track performance, but Cossalter concedes there were compromises elsewhere. “Customers told us the old Performante wasn’t comfortable enough, especially in the back. We have solved that problem by using air suspension, rather than steel springs.”

The ‘SE’ part of the new car’s name is also important. It denotes the plug-in hybrid hardware – a 25.9kWh battery and rear e-motor – that contributes an extra 192hp. This makes this Performante appreciably more powerful than its predecessor, and better at the multi-tasking demanded of an SUV. Along with scorching to 62mph in 3.3 seconds and a top speed of 194mph, it can travel up to 40 miles using battery power alone. On paper at least, you can have your panettone and eat it,

Engineered for extroverts 

In the metal, any thoughts of this being a sensible family SUV quickly evaporate – especially if your Performante is finished in the highlighter-pen yellow seen here, officially known as Giallo Crius. It looks like a car that guzzles raw eggs for breakfast, a Huel smoothie for lunch and a bloodied steak for dinner, washed down with several cans of Monster. Haters are gonna hate, but ever since the Miura defined the supercar in 1966, Lamborghinis have never blended into the background. Introverts need not apply. 

You can tell the Performante apart from a common-or-garden Urus SE by its twin front S-ducts, which resemble 911 GT3-style nostrils. Look closer and you’ll also spot wider air intakes, a new splitter, angular wheelarch extensions and a second rear spoiler. Many of the exterior panels are made from carbon fibre, including the bonnet, sill covers and rear bumper/diffuser. Indeed, Lamborghini claims this is ‘the SUV with the widest use of carbon fibre in the world’.  

That may be so, but a total weight loss of 32kg – by the time you factor in a new titanium exhaust system (saving 10kg) and lighter Corsa Tex upholstery (2.7kg) – is pretty inconsequential in a vehicle that tips the scales at 2,473kg. The old, non-hybrid Urus Performante was more than 300kg lighter. 

In more positive news, the new Performante is actually three percent more aerodynamic than its standard SE sibling, while also delivering a 23 percent increase in maximum downforce. It rides on 22-inch wheels, which can be wrapped in Bridgestone Potenza Race tyres (fitted here), just in case you fancy attempting a Nurburgring record of your own. Larger 23-inch rims with road-focused Pirelli rubber are on the options list

Inside the Urus SE Performante

If you do plan a weekend away at the Nordschleife, of course, you can take the kids and cocker spaniel along for the ride. The Performante might be at the extreme end of the SUV spectrum, but it’s no less practical than any Urus SE, with five seats and 414 litres of luggage space (down from 616 litres in the original car, due to the hybrid batteries beneath the boot floor). 

The cabin looks almost as angular as the exterior, with an abundance of Lamborghini’s signature hexagons and the bulky ‘Tamburo’ drive mode selector atop the centre console. New for the SE Performante is a Rally mode – perhaps inspired by the brilliant Huracan Sterrato – which is designed for driving fast on dirt or gravel roads. The usual Strada, Sport and Corsa settings are present and correct, too. 

A 12.3-inch central touchscreen handles the infotainment, including wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity, with a separate screen for the heating and ventilation controls underneath. Thankfully, there are also plenty of tactile physical switches, while quality is as good as you’d hope for a car that takes on the Aston Martin DBX S and Bentley Bentayga Speed.  

The fastest SUV, but only just

Lamborghini says the ultra-Urus is the ‘fastest SUV in the world’, although it depends on your definition of the F-word. Yes, its 194mph top speed beats the Aston Martin, Bentley and Ferrari Purosangue by a small-but-significant 1mph. However, another SUV from the Volkswagen Group stable, the new Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric, is much quicker off the mark – hitting 62mph in just 2.5 seconds.

Still, no-one will clamber out of an Urus SE Performante thinking it feels a bit lethargic. The combination of instant battery torque, four-wheel drive and those sticky Bridgestones makes a launch-control start feel gut-wrenching, then the big-lunged V8 piles on speed relentlessly. On Vairano’s two-kilometre straight, it will blast beyond 150mph with ease.

It makes noises that no EV can match, too. The Akrapovic exhaust sounds less explosive than you might expect, despite Lamborghini’s promise of ‘more backfire sounds’. No doubt many owners will fit aftermarket pipes. However, the twin-turbo engine bellows like Brian Blessed, its tone fuller and more resonant than the flat-plane V8 in the Temerario. If your experience of hybrids thus far is limited to Uber rides in a Toyota Prius, prepare to have your preconceptions blown apart.  

Take it to the track

Equally, if you’re used to driving a not-so-super SUV, the way the Urus goes around corners may frazzle your brain. Taxes introduced in response to temporary pressures have a habit of outlasting them. The Chancellor must keep his promise that the bank tax rise is only temporary, writes David Postings 

After weeks of speculation in the run-up to the Budget, the Chancellor stood at the despatch box and praised the UK’s world-leading banks for the tax they pay and the jobs and investment they support. But he then doubled the bank corporation tax surcharge from three to six per cent. The Chancellor promised that the increase would last for only 15 months, and HM Treasury has stated that the time limit will be written into legislation.

He was right about the industry’s contribution. Banking is a vital part of the UK economy, and one I have been proud to be involved in for almost 50 years. Banks help people buy homes, support businesses to invest and grow, and already contribute billions of pounds in tax every year. They are major employers and major sources of investment right across the country, helping to drive growth in every postcode.

Every Chancellor faces difficult choices and competing demands on the public finances. But increasing taxes on banks is not the way to drive growth or enhance the UK’s international competitiveness.

The higher rate will apply from January 2027 to the end of March 2028. The fact that the increase is time-limited matters. It provides some reassurance to an industry making investment and lending decisions over many years. But that reassurance will hold only if the government honours the promised end date.

Energy Profits Levy is a case study in trusting ‘temporary measures’

History gives us reason to be cautious. Taxes introduced in response to temporary pressures have a habit of lasting longer than originally intended.

The Energy Profits Levy is a recent example. It was introduced as a temporary measure and was originally due to end by December 2025, but its rate has been increased and its duration extended.

Banks have also seen sector-specific taxation become an established part of the UK tax system. The bank levy has been in place since 2011, while the bank corporation tax surcharge has applied since 2016. Over the longer term, the government should be looking to reduce this additional burden, not increase it.

This is not an abstract concern. International firms decide where to deploy capital and create jobs. A stable and predictable tax regime is one important factor in those decisions.

Other countries are moving in the opposite direction. Banks in the EU Banking Union contributed to the Single Resolution Fund until it reached its required level. No regular annual contributions have been collected since 2024. This lowered the total tax rate on banks operating in countries such as Germany. Germany is also reducing its corporate income tax rate by one percentage point a year between 2028 and 2032. Its government has been explicit that the purpose is to make Germany more competitive and attractive to international investment.

The UK cannot take its position as a leading global financial centre for granted, particularly when our competitors are working hard to attract business.

The government’s Financial Services Growth and Competitiveness Strategy set an ambition for the UK to be the global location of choice for financial services firms looking to invest, innovate and grow. A higher and less predictable tax burden pulls in the opposite direction.

The Chancellor has made a clear promise that the increase will end after 15 months.

Having introduced a tax rise that does not support growth or competitiveness, we will be watching closely to ensure that a promise made is a promise kept.

The ballooning benefits bill, the terrifying lack of economic growth, our inadequate defence programme: Labour’s Budget had nothing to offer for Britain’s biggest issues, writes Emma Revell

Word on the street ahead of John Healey’s first Budget was that the mantra in Whitehall when preparing the document was “do no harm”. Unfortunately for the country, mandarins and Treasury boffins seem to have confused that idea with “do as little as humanly possible”. In seeking to do no harm, Healey did at least, as my colleague Robert Colvile put it on Budget day, “ignore many of the more lunatic ideas being proposed by his parliamentary colleagues” but that doesn’t mean he has actually done anyone any good.

The biggest challenges facing Britain are our terrifying lack of economic growth, the ballooning size of the benefits bill, the ticking time bomb that is serving our national debt and the total inadequacy of our defence programme, for which John Healey has already resigned once.

The Budget ignored them all. 

On welfare, Healey has been able to hide behind Labour grandee Alan Milburn and his as-yet-unfinished review into the rise of workless young people. While there is every chance Milburn will make serious recommendations into how to tackle this issue, it is one narrow element of the overall problem we have with the benefits bill and with worklessness, and one Labour has explicitly contributed to by hiking up the minimum wage to the ludicrous point where a 21-year-old working full-time on the minimum wage is already half way towards being a higher rate tax payer. Milburn’s focus on young people won’t address worklessness in older people, or the massive surge in health-related benefits driving much of the increased spending. Nor will anything he says likely prevent Labour backbenchers or the campaigning classes adjacent to Labour activists from fighting tooth and nail against even the mildest benefit reforms. 

Healey also kicked the can down the road on defence, maintaining departmental budgets at the level previously set out by Rachel Reeves – give or take a billion a year which the Conservatives are claiming is a cut in defence spending but the government insist is just an accounting measure, moving pensions spending to the Treasury rather than sitting with the Ministry of Defence. Instead we were told that details on how the government will increase spending to 3.0 per cent, then 3.5 per cent of GDP, and get our Armed Forces in a position to tackle the very real threats that seem to be mounting up – whether from Russia, the Middle East, or stateless AI-powered terror – would come ahead of next year’s Spending Review.

Was this a pre-election Budget?

Labour likes to talk about growth, and on occasion you feel as if certain members of the Cabinet do actually understand what it means to get growth back into the economy. Sadly they, and governments for the last two decades, have enacted policies which almost seem designed not to give us any. The general public likely do not comprehend how poor our growth has been since the financial crisis but The Prosperity Alliance calculated that if growth had continued along pre-2008 trends the median household would be £16,000 a year better off. Yet the Budget contained no measures that even come close to driving growth – even the trade bodies name-checked by the Chancellor in his Budget speech as supportive of some of the smaller measures announced had little positive to say overall.

The CBI said the Budget “lacks the bold moves” needed to make businesses’ lives easier, the FSB rightly pointed out there was “nothing to ease sky-high energy bills” and the British Chambers of Commerce said the announcements lacked “the big calls that would really shift the economic dial”.

If you are inclined to be generous, you could say John Healey did a good job of avoiding the summer of misery inflicted upon the economy by Rachel Reeves’ two Budgets. This summer didn’t include months of drip-fed headlines about black holes and enormous tax rises, but if not spooking the bond markets ahead of the Budget is the best you can hope for, we really are setting the bar low. It would also be fair to point out some measures that would dramatically boost growth sit outside the remit of a budget. 

Unfortunately, our economic situation is so dire we cannot afford to give Labour the benefit of the doubt. A Budget utterly lacking in vision, peppered with small retail offerings designed to appeal to the public and paper over the cracks can only mean one of two things: Labour has no stomach for the difficult decisions needed to save us, or Andy Burnham has urged his Chancellor to postpone those decisions until after an early general election. 

As disruptive and depressing as the latter might be, and as much as Burnham might deny that is his plan, the idea that we are trapped with a government bereft of ideas and lacking in gumption is so unpalatable even Brenda from Bristol might hope we’ll soon be going to the polls.

Emma Revell is external affairs director at the Centre for Policy Studies

The watchdog on Thursday identified four methods it considers sufficiently reliable to determine whether users are aged 16 or over, ahead of the restrictions coming into force in March.

The proposals would affect some of the UK’s biggest social media platforms, including Instagram, Tiktok and Snapchat, with many adult users also likely to face checks before continuing to access their accounts.

Ofcom said photo ID matching, banking-based checks, digital ID services and facial age estimation could all meet its standards, although it acknowledged that some children would inevitably find ways around the restrictions.

“This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right”, said Ofcom chief executive Dame Melanie Dawes.

“When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply”.

Millions face age checks

The recommendations expose the practical difficulties facing tech firms as they prepare to distinguish 15-year-olds from 16-year-olds.

Ofcom warned that some facial age estimation systems can be inaccurate by several years, meaning platforms may need to request additional identification from users whose ages cannot be reliably determined.

The regulator suggested adopting an approach similar to retailers’ Challenge 25 policy, requiring further proof of age where uncertainty remains.

Around 150,000 British 16- and 17-year-olds are estimated to have neither a passport nor a driving licence, potentially forcing some teenagers to obtain identification to retain their accounts.

Meanwhile, roughly 90 per cent of people in that age group have a bank account, offering another route to verification.

Georgina Graham, a partner at law firm Osborne Clarke, said: “Requirements to implement highly effective age assurance and to protect user privacy are not inherently incompatible. It is completely possible to do both”.

However, she warned that differing rules across countries could complicate compliance for technology firms operating internationally.

The recommendations will now be considered by ministers, who are expected to publish detailed regulations before the end of the year.

Platforms face enforcement challenge

The proposals come amid concerns that Britain’s ban could suffer the same problems as Australia’s restrictions, where children have continued accessing social media despite being prohibited from doing so.

Ofcom acknowledged that circumvention could not be eliminated entirely, but said platforms should introduce measures to detect underage accounts and allow users to report suspected breaches.

Research from EE found that 42 per cent of young people plan to get around the ban by moving to apps outside its scope, while 44 per cent have already discussed alternatives with friends.

Andy Lulham, chief operating officer at age verification firm VerifyMy, said the challenge would be particularly acute for teenagers.

“Estimation needs a threshold built in, and the borderline cases are a genuine trade-off between the occasional 15-year-old getting through and some 16-year-olds being turned away”, he said.

Ofcom also turned its attention to app stores, warning that their reliance on users declaring their own ages offered insufficient protection.

Its research found that three-quarters of children who use the internet primarily access it through apps downloaded from app stores.

Tech companies like Meta have previously argued that age checks should be conducted at device or app-store level, shifting some responsibility towards Apple and Google.

However, Ofcom insisted that social media platforms would remain responsible for meeting their own legal obligations, regardless of additional safeguards introduced elsewhere.

Chancellor John Healey’s decision to overhaul the self-assessment tax system has sparked concerns among tax advisers, as they question whether this will harm Britain’s self-employed.

Healey confirmed in his maiden Autumn Budget that the government will change how income tax self-assessment (ITSA) taxpayers make their Payments on Accounts.

Payments on Account are advance payments made by roughly one quarter of self employed Brits, according to Travers Smith. 

Under current rules, this group does not pay tax as they earn income over the course of the financial year, instead paying an estimated portion in advance every six months based on previous year’s earnings.

As tax bills aren’t typically due until ten months after the end of the tax year, self-employed workers can face up to a 22 month delay between earning income and settling the tax owed with HMRC. Payment on Account enables HMRC to close the gap and prevent taxpayers from facing a substantial, delayed bill.

From April 2029, this system will be replaced with smaller, regular in-year payments made as income is earned. 

Creating a cash crunch?

Advisers across the City have clashed over Healey’s decision, with some arguing the change will negatively impact those with “fluctuating incomes” and instead give HMRC “a big cashflow advantage at the cost of taxpayers”.

“Bringing forward Self Assessment payments might seem harmless because the amount of tax people pay stays the same, but it could leave many short of cash,” said David Portman, tax partner at Lubbock Fine.

“Lawyers and accountants are likely to be among the hardest hit because the amount of tax they pay each year can be significant… as well as those with significant savings income.”

Other advisers noted it will create a “significant cashflow challenge” for tradesmen as well as white collar professionals, including plumbers, electricians and farmers, alongside investors and landlords, and could cause some businesses to close their doors.

Andy Oury, tax partner at Oury Clark, said: “It’s been my fear that accelerated payments was always the grander design… That will be a one-off working capital transfer from the bank accounts of plumbers, cleaners and coders into the Exchequer, dressed up as helping people budget and avoiding larger tax bills that are harder to pay.”

“But the transition will be brutal. It will mean roughly eighteen months of tax squeezed into twelve. This could be a solvency event for some.”

Advisers urged the government to consider delaying the proposal or implement a phased introduction, to “allow them to gradually bring their payments forward” and stop workers running out of capital in 2029.

The case for HMRC

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates the measure to generate £1.6bn on average annually from the 2029/30 tax year, driven partly by reductions in debt losses and by bringing forward the timing of tax recovery.

“The announcement signals a continued focus on strengthening HMRC’s ability to recover unpaid tax, particularly from individuals who have the means to settle their liabilities but repeatedly fail to engage,” said Andy Wood, barrister at Tax Barrister UK.

Tom Everett, tax partner at PwC, added the changes may “make budgeting easier” for some taxpayers, by bringing payment closer to when income is actually earned.

But many advisers questioned what safeguards HMRC will implement to protect taxpayers, as the Budget failed to provide details on how the change will be brought into effect.

Adam Jefferies, Director in the Private Client Tax team at PKF Littlejohn: “With key details still unclear, there are concerns over increased red tape and taxpayers being hit with bills based on out-of-date information.”

Hundreds of thousands of low-income pensioners are set to pay an effective 53 per cent tax rate on part of their retirement income, under new rules introduced by John Healey in his maiden Budget.

The Chancellor confirmed he will shield low-income pensioners from income tax as the state pension is set to rise above the personal allowance threshold from April 2027.

The full state benefit will rise by £489 to £13,036, pushing those who rely solely on the benefit above the £12,570 threshold. Healey hiked the threshold to the new amount to ensure the UK’s poorest retirees do not pay income tax.

But for those who earn just above this income level, the tax rate will be reduced by £1 for every £3 of income above the threshold. The mechanism acts as a benefit taper, similar to the 60 per cent tax rate, as extra income causes the temporary relief to be wiped away.

For pensioners on £13,319 or above, the tax break will therefore be reduced to zero.

Buckling other low earners

While the policy protects those under the threshold, those who earn between that range will face an effective tax rate of 53 per cent, according to pensions consultant LCP.

The rate is made up of 20 per cent basic income tax rate, plus the loss of the tax break at 33 per cent.

Steve Webb, partner at LCP and former pensions minister, said retirees will find that each £100 of annual private pension built above the rate of the new state guarantee will add £53 to their income tax bill.

“The Chancellor has created a bizarre 53 per cent income tax rate for around 200,000 low income pensioners,” he said.

“We are used to seeing high rates of income tax like this for top earners but not for those on very modest incomes. Yet again, complexity has been introduced to the tax system to fix a short-term problem but with no long-term solution in mind.”

The wide gap

Advisers warned Healey not to introduce the policy, as the gap between the new state pension and frozen tax threshold will continue to widen over the course of this Parliament, making it harder to “switch off”.

The gap will grow by a minimum of 2.5 per cent annually, putting a further burden on the public purse. It is expected to cost taxpayers £200m a year by 2030.

In the 2027/28 tax year, the state guarantee is expected to rise to £250.70 per week, leaving it £466.40 above the threshold.

Rose, who took the helm last year after joining from Microsoft, has been tasked with reviving the advertising group following years of declining performance, client losses and mounting competition from rivals.

Her three-year turnaround strategy – dubbed Elevate28 – aims to simplify WPP’s sprawling network of agencies, cut costs and return the business to growth in 2027.

“We are on track to deliver phase one of Elevate28: stabilising our business performance and laying the foundations for a simpler, more unified WPP”, Rose said.

“Our third quarter results show further sequential improvement in LFL growth, in line with our expectations.”

The group secured a string of major client wins and renewals during the quarter, including Coca-Cola, Doordash, Nestlé, Uber and Google’s self-driving car business Waymo.

Rose said demand remained healthy for WPP’s AI-powered advertising services, including its agentic marketing platform WPP Open, as the industry grapples with the growing influence of AI on creative production and media buying.

The company has also opened a new AI-enabled production facility in east London and expanded its data partnerships as it seeks to compete more effectively with tech companies entering the advertising market.

Cost cuts continue

WPP’s latest update follows a bruising first half in which the company cut another 1,267 jobs, bringing its workforce reduction over the preceding 12 months to 6.4 per cent.

The group has been shedding staff and simplifying its agency structure as part of plans to deliver £500m in cost savings by the end of 2028.

It expects to achieve £100m in savings this year, alongside approximately £250m in restructuring costs.

WPP also reiterated plans to generate at least £200m from asset disposals as it seeks to strengthen its balance sheet.

Its adjusted net debt stood at £3bn at the end of September, down from £3.6bn a year earlier.

Despite the improving quarterly performance, WPP remains under pressure to demonstrate that its restructuring can deliver sustained growth.

The company has lost its position as the world’s largest advertising holding group to France’s Publicis, while the rapid adoption of AI is forcing traditional agencies to rethink how they deliver services.

Rose said WPP was preparing for the next phase of its turnaround, with the aim of returning to organic growth during 2027.

Casino operator Rank Group has warned that John Healey’s gambling tax hike will deliver a hit of around £9m a year, as the industry begins to count the cost of Wednesday’s Budget.

The London-listed owner of Grosvenor Casinos and Mecca Bingo said the increase in Machine Games Duty (MGD) from 20 to 25 per cent, which takes effect in April 2027, would add approximately £9m to its annual tax bill before any measures to offset the impact.

Rank expects an additional £2m in costs during its current financial year, ending June 2027, but said it remained confident of delivering like-for-like operating profit in line with expectations.

The company said it would provide further details of the Budget’s impact and its plans to mitigate the costs alongside its half-year results on 28 January.

Gambling firms count the cost

Rank’s warning comes a day after gambling stocks rallied on relief that the Chancellor had opted for a smaller tax increase than many in the industry had feared.

Shares in Rank jumped eight per cent on Wednesday, while Ladbrokes owner Entain gained more than six per cent and William Hill owner Evoke rose nearly four per cent.

Campaigners and some Labour MPs had pushed for MGD to rise to 40 per cent, but Healey settled on 25 per cent.

Entain has already estimated that the increase will cost its UK retail business £25m annually before mitigation, although it expects to offset the impact by the end of 2028 through shop closures, cost savings and market share gains.

The Betting and Gaming Council (BGC) warned that almost 1,000 betting shops and casinos could close or face serious financial pressure as a result of the tax changes, citing modelling commissioned from EY.

“This is a deeply damaging decision and a blow to the thousands of workers, businesses and communities who depend on Britain’s regulated betting and gaming industry”, said BGC chief executive Grainne Hurst.

“The Chancellor has ignored repeated warnings about the consequences”.

The increase adds to mounting pressure on high street gambling operators, following last year’s rise in Remote Gaming Duty on online casino profits to 40 per cent.

General Betting Duty on online sports betting is also set to rise to 25 per cent next April.

While the smaller-than-feared MGD increase offered investors some relief, Rank’s latest figures underline the additional costs facing operators as the changes take effect.

Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:13:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

The first profit, and how thin it was

That changed with the 2025 financial year. According to Bolt’s own results, reported in coverage from Trade with Estonia, the company took €2.27 billion in revenue across more than 50 countries, a 14 percent increase on the year before, and posted its first-ever annual net profit: €920,000. Set against €2.27 billion in revenue, that works out to a margin of roughly four hundredths of one percent, the kind of number that is technically profitable and not much more. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. Villig described the underlying business as having reached a $14 billion gross merchandise value run-rate with two consecutive years of positive cash flow, arguably the more meaningful signal for a company at Bolt’s stage than the net income line itself.

What a four-hundredths-of-a-percent margin actually means

A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. The accounts do not reveal whether Bolt targeted that result or whether it could sustain growth without further external financing. They show a small net profit and positive operating cash flow for the year, not permanent financial independence. It hasn’t settled every question that scale raises, either.

In November 2024, a UK employment tribunal ruled that Bolt’s drivers qualify as workers rather than independent contractors — a ruling on status only, with compensation still to be set at a separate hearing. Leigh Day, the law firm representing roughly 15,000 drivers in the claim, estimates the compensation owed could exceed £200 million, or upwards of £15,000 per driver on average, according to Leigh Day’s own statement. Whether a margin this thin holds, thickens, or gets eaten by exactly that kind of regulatory ruling as Bolt pushes into new cities, verticals and eventually autonomous vehicles is the open question its 2025 results don’t settle either way.

Correction, 1 October 2026: The original excerpt called Estonia the world leader, although the cited per-capita tally places it second behind Liechtenstein. The article also misstated the Tiger Leap school-internet rollout; first-party history says all schools were connected by 2001.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The one that started it

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

Why the count kept growing

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

A pipeline that keeps producing, even without unicorns

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. Estonian startups collectively reported €3.9 billion in revenue in 2024, up 14.7 percent on the year before, according to Invest in Estonia’s own sector figures, and the sector now employs about 14,400 people directly, or roughly one in every 38 working Estonians, at an average monthly salary of €3,650, more than double the national average. Venture capital raised by Estonian startups actually fell 23 percent in 2024, to €326.6 million across 57 rounds, the lowest total in five years, a reminder that a dense unicorn count doesn’t insulate a small ecosystem from a broader European slowdown in early-stage funding. What has held up is the type of company being funded: deep technology, rather than consumer apps or fintech, took 63 percent of all startup investment in 2024, led by rounds for the delivery-robot company Starship Technologies and the green-hydrogen firm Stargate Hydrogen.

What the density figure doesn’t tell you

A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

Milda Mitkutė was changing apartments in Vilnius in 2008 and had more clothes than the new place could hold. Rather than throw them out, she wanted a way to pass them on to people she knew. A friend, the software developer Justas Janauskas, built her a website for it. “We chatted about creating a website where people could trade their pre-loved fashion with each other,” Janauskas later told Tech.eu in 2015, recalling that he was doubtful the idea would go anywhere until he asked around and found most of his friends thought it was a good one.

The two of them built the earliest version as a side project, under a Lithuanian name that translated roughly to “my clothes,” with no marketing budget and no plan beyond friends trading with friends. What tipped it into something larger was almost accidental. A couch-surfing guest from Munich learned about the site, liked it, and helped carry the idea into Germany, where it launched under its own local name, Kleiderkreisel. Other country-specific spin-offs followed the same pattern for a few years, each with its own name and its own small user base, before the company folded them together under a single brand, Vinted, as the parent business decided a fragmented set of local sites made less sense than one platform users could recognise anywhere in Europe. Vilnius stayed its home throughout.

How a free listing site turns a profit

The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Vinted makes its money almost entirely from the buyer’s side of the transaction: a fixed fee of roughly $0.70 plus a variable fee of about 5 percent of the item’s price, charged in the buyer’s local currency (figures as of late 2025) — according to Vinted’s own Buyer Protection fee page. That fee funds Vinted’s Buyer Protection service, including secure payment handling and dispute support. Shipping is a separate charge paid by the buyer at checkout, even though the seller receives a prepaid label. It is close to the inverse of how rivals like Poshmark and Depop have historically operated, charging the seller a cut instead. Vinted also sells optional promotion to sellers who want more visibility: a feature called Closet Spotlight puts five of a seller’s listings into other users’ feeds for a week for a flat fee, and a per-item “bump” pushes a single listing up in search results, priced dynamically by category and demand.

From a hobby site to a logistics network

Underneath the fee structure sits a harder problem: getting a stranger’s old jumper from a seller’s flat to a buyer’s front door, cheaply and reliably, across dozens of countries. That has turned Vinted into as much a logistics company as a marketplace. According to the company’s own 2025 financial results, its delivery partner network now gives users access to more than 500,000 pick-up and drop-off points across Europe, and the company runs its own parcel carrier, Vinted Go, directly in five markets: Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain. The money that built out Vinted’s logistics network came in stages, and the pace of it tracks how quickly investors decided the model was working. In November 2019, the company raised €128 million in a round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, with Accel, Insight Partners, Sprints Capital and Burda Principal Investments also participating, pushing its valuation past $1 billion for the first time and making it, according to the reporting on the round, Lithuania’s first unicorn. Lightspeed partner Brad Twohig said at the time the firm looked for “outlier management teams building generational companies,” a fairly standard line for a venture press release, but one that in this case was describing two people who had started out solving a problem for their own friends.

Two years later, in 2021, a further round led by EQT Growth brought in $303 million and roughly quadrupled the valuation again, to $4.5 billion, with the same core group of earlier investors returning. That was the last outside funding round before the company turned its first profit in 2023, at which point continued growth could increasingly be funded from the business itself rather than from new investors.

What the 2025 numbers actually show

Vinted’s first profitable year, by its own account, was 2023, when it reported revenue of €596.3 million and a net profit of €17.8 million, a milestone The Next Web covered as the company’s first since founding. Two years later, the picture is bigger but less straightforwardly better. Vinted moved €10.8 billion in gross merchandise value in 2025, up 47 percent on the year before, and took €1.1 billion of that as revenue, up 38 percent, almost double the 2023 figure. That is a company reinvesting in expansion while remaining profitable, not a company in trouble. It is worth naming the distinction because the two can look similar on a spreadsheet, and a 19 percent drop in profit reads very differently once it’s clear the company was profitable at all only two years earlier, and is still profitable now, just less so by design.

A platform built on other people’s closets

What the €10.8 billion figure represents is how far secondhand clothing has moved from a hobby into ordinary consumer behaviour across Europe. The company has said it intends to bring the same model to the United States next, according to Dealroom’s coverage of the 2025 results. Whether Vinted’s European logistics playbook, built over seventeen years and hundreds of thousands of parcel points, transfers to a market with a completely different postal and returns infrastructure is the open question the 2025 numbers don’t answer.
