  • Power for hard ground: The system includes a 97 kW (130 hp) engine and a high-frequency hydraulic hammer with up to 1,260 J (929 ft.-lb.) of impact energy and three energy settings to match soil conditions.

]]> Swedish AI startup Pixel Systems has raised €2.7 million ($3.1 million) in a Seed round to accelerate their commercial initiatives and continue building the technology that helps identify AI-generated and manipulated images, documents, and other digital material.

The round was led by Unconventional Ventures, at a pre-money valuation of approximately €18 million ($21 million).

“Generative AI has made it extremely cheap to fabricate evidence. The problem is that almost every digital process still rests on the assumption that what people submit is authentic. That assumption is disappearing,” says Robel Efrem, co-founder and CEO of Pixel.

Pixel’s funding follows other European investments in digital trust and fraud-prevention technology reported by EU-Startups in 2026, including Sweden’s Bits (€12 million), Denmark’s Flare (€3.6 million), France’s Marble (€6.5 million) and MokN (€12.9 million), Spain’s Zepo Intelligence (€12.8 million), and UK/Germany-based Diligent AI (€2.1 million).

Together, these rounds represent approximately €49.9 million in funding, excluding Pixel’s €2.7 million Seed round, across companies addressing different aspects of verification, fraud prevention and financial crime.

EU-Startups previously covered Efrem as co-founder and CEO of Swedish esports platform Challengermode, which raised €10.1 million in 2020.

“We believe the ability to verify digital information will become as natural a part of tomorrow’s infrastructure as cybersecurity is today. That a Swedish company has the opportunity to take a leading position in this field is exactly the kind of development we want to help make possible,” adds Nora Bavey, General Partner at Unconventional Ventures.

Founded in 2026 in Stockholm, Pixel develops proprietary technology to detect AI-generated and manipulated digital content. By combining several independent forensic analysis methods, Pixel helps companies verify images, documents, and other digital material before it is used as the basis for decisions, payouts, or other critical processes.

The team behind Pixel consists of senior engineers, AI specialists, and competitive programmers.

In Pixel’s internal tests, the platform has achieved a detection rate of 99.98 percent for AI-generated and manipulated material, reportedly placing the technology at a world-leading level.

Pixel is used today in businesses where digital material forms the basis for financial decisions, including insurance, FinTech, e-commerce, and professional services.

Use cases include manipulated damage photos in insurance claims, fabricated receipts and invoices, AI-generated product images in refund fraud, and manipulated material in financial or legal processes.

“The internet was built for a world where an image could largely be treated as proof. That world no longer exists. Now every company that receives images, receipts, and documents from its customers needs to be able to check that material before money is paid out,” says Robel Efrem.

The funding comes just months after the company was founded. Three weeks after its commercial launch, Pixel has reached its first €89k ($100k) in contracted recurring revenue.

]]> A friend of mine runs a company that builds software for other companies. He has the same problem in most sales meetings. He shows what the system can do, the prospect leans forward and asks how it works, and my friend, who is not daft, goes slightly vague. If he explains it properly, they might go away and build it themselves.

Some of them go away and build it anyway. About a year later, a fair number rang back and asked for help.

So there is still money in knowing how to make something work. What AI has done is make the gap between a clever demo and a defensible company rather uncomfortable to look at. The tools that let your team build sophisticated software cheaply let a competitor rebuild it cheaply too, and your customers can have a go over a long weekend. The development bill has come down for everyone. That includes the people trying to put you out of business.

Your supplier has a product team too

In my previous article, I asked what would happen to a startup if its model disappeared tomorrow. There is a quieter version of that dependency. The supplier carries on answering your API calls and starts selling what you sell.

On 24 February, Anthropic released finance plugins for Claude covering equity research, investment banking, private equity and wealth management, with workflows that run across Excel and PowerPoint. If you were selling an AI equity research assistant on 23 February, you had a new slide to write for your next board meeting.

Figma had it worse. On 17 February, it announced an integration with Claude Code, letting interfaces built in Claude drop straight onto the Figma canvas. On 17 April, Anthropic launched Claude Design, which produces interface mockups and interactive prototypes. Three days earlier, Anthropic’s chief product officer had stepped down from Figma’s board, which, in hindsight, was something of a hint. Figma’s shares fell 7% on launch day. Presumably the next partnership meeting had a slightly different atmosphere.

You may also be using that provider’s tools to build the product it is about to replace. I wouldn’t hold that against anyone. I would just keep it in mind.

Somebody else’s high street

In February 2025, Chegg, which sells homework help to students, reported that its non-subscriber traffic for January was down 49%, against a decline of 8% in the second quarter of 2024. It blamed Google’s AI Overviews for answering the questions that used to send students to its site, and sued Google that same week. That is Chegg’s account, and Google disputes it. The shape of the problem reaches well beyond homework.

The platform that sends customers to your door can start answering their questions on the doorstep. You still have a website. Fewer people have a reason to visit it.

Before anyone talks about a moat, it is worth checking how much of the surrounding land you actually own.

Six months used to be a moat

A feature that once took six months of engineering may now take a fraction of that. Marvellous, until you realise those six months were most of what kept the competition out.

Customers do the same sum. Some will decide their own developers can rebuild enough of your product in-house. They will underestimate the maintenance and the awkward exceptions, as my friend’s returning clients did. Their attempt still costs him a year of sales, and he doesn’t get the year back when they ring.

So where is the moat?

It starts with knowing how to get a better result. It deepens with the things you learn that a competitor can’t pick up by watching your demo.

Take my own industry. Getting an AI to produce a plausible trade recommendation is easy to show on stage. Getting software to behave inside a broker’s real trading infrastructure is another matter. Permissions have to hold when an instruction is ambiguous; someone has to reconcile the books when a transaction fails halfway through. None of this appears in the sales presentation. It turns up in the third week of production, usually on a Monday.

A competitor can copy your screen without knowing how you handle any of that. A customer can build a prototype without ever finding out why your production version took so long.

Proprietary data helps, provided you actually have the rights to use it. A pile of public documents anyone can download offers rather less protection. Calling it a knowledge base does not make it yours.

The test is simple enough. If someone offered your visible features at half the price, would your customers stay? “We shipped first” is not an answer.

Make sure you can change the engine

Whatever the advantage is, it has to survive a change of model. 

Founders should know what they would run instead of their current provider, and whether it is good enough on their customers’ actual work. Benchmarks are not customers. For some applications, an open-weight model hosted in-house is the sensible answer.

Buying a server does not give you a moat. It does stop a supplier’s product roadmap from closing your company.

If switching providers would strip out everything your customers value, then the valuable part was never yours. You were renting it.

Whose moat does regulation dig?

This is also why I am skeptical of calls for an AI slowdown. A voluntary pause is hard to hold when competitors keep building and customers can leave. The data centres still need paying for.

Regulation can do something a voluntary pause can’t. It can make getting in more expensive.

A large provider spreads the cost of compliance across a business that already exists. A startup has to find that money before it has much revenue. Rules that make independent models prohibitively expensive would leave smaller companies even more dependent on the suppliers already eating into their margins.

There are good reasons to regulate AI. But when the biggest providers ask for more rules, I’d like to know who can afford to follow them. A requirement their legal department absorbs before lunch may be enough to stop a smaller competitor getting funded at all.

Europe’s AI Act makes some allowances for this, including exemptions for certain open-source models. Much depends on the detail. Writing rules that only the largest companies can afford to follow is an excellent way of keeping them the largest companies.

What they were paying for

Founders should assume cheaper development means more competition. The defence has to be something that grows every time you serve a customer and is still standing after the next model release.

Clients came back because copying the idea was easier than delivering the result. AI made their first attempt cheaper. It did not give them the vendor’s experience. They saved on development and spent a year finding out what they had been paying for.

The pattern is familiar. An internal team looks at a vendor’s product and concludes it could be rebuilt in a couple of sprints. Occasionally, it can. More often, the organisation pays for the lesson twice: once in the build, and again in the operational gaps that only appear in production.

]]> Bleu Robotics, a Paris-based startup building AI models for industrial humanoid robots, has raised a €5 million pre-Seed round, to reach its goal of reducing the full humanoid robot deployment process to one hour or shorter.

The round was co-led by Contrarian Ventures and OVNI Capital, with participation from Kvanted, WEPA Ventures, Motier Ventures and Charlie Songhurst, and board members at Meta.

Benoît Berkoukchi, co-founder of Bleu Robotics, says, “Humanoid robots in manufacturing are the next automotive sector, with the potential to help Europe and the US reshore production. But most robotics companies are trying to train humanoids with millions of data points and build fully general-purpose models. That approach isn’t suited to manufacturing. There isn’t enough data on factory work, and there won’t be internet-scale data, the kind LLMs were built on, for robots for a long time. Our methodology means we can do more with less.”

The round comes amid continued European investment in robotics software, humanoid systems and Physical AI during 2026.

In France, Paris-based Inbolt raised €11 million to expand its hardware-agnostic robot intelligence platform, while Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics secured €26 million to develop AI-powered skills for industrial robots.

Elsewhere, Belgium’s Motion raised €1.7 million for humanoid deployment, Spain’s THEKER secured €73 million to scale generalist industrial robotics, and London-based Humanoid raised €133 million for its industrial humanoid platform.

Together with funding rounds for Germany’s Sereact, Switzerland’s Enact Intelligence and Poland’s Nomagic, these financings total €372.7 million in 2026, rising to €377.7 million when including Bleu Robotics’ latest round.

Thomas Poitrineau, Investor at Contrarian Ventures, adds, “We were attracted to Bleu Robotics because of their ambitious choice to rethink how humanoid robotics software should work from first principles. It’s rare to find a company led by two world-class robotics researchers and a manufacturing expert, which is also why their software works differently from their competition. Their goal is far bigger than simply making the best model in a lab. It’s an approach that can already scale, putting robots to work in factories within months rather than years.”

Founded in Paris in 2025 by two INRIA researchers and a former Renault manufacturing manager, Bleu’s abductive learning technology reportedly lets robots learn new tasks from only a handful of operator demonstrations.

Its software runs on any humanoid platform and includes the AI model and training devices needed to teach robots on the factory floor.

According to the International Federation of Robotics, there were 5 million industrial robots operating globally in 2025. However, these robots are built to repeat fixed tasks, and are unable to adapt to the high-mix, low-volume production now common in modern manufacturing, so that work still falls to human workers.

Humanoid robots are needed to automate a wider range of complex tasks. While hardware has advanced significantly in recent years, software development has struggled to keep pace, limiting real-world deployment.

Interact Analysis found that of the 20,000-plus humanoids produced last year, only 10% reached real-world applications. Most of these robots today rely on end-to-end models, which learn everything in a single black box and require massive amounts of data to achieve production-ready reliability.

As a result, deployment remains costly and time-consuming for manufacturers, often requiring hundreds of hours of training data, with no guarantee the robot will perform reliably.

Instead of an end-to-end model, Bleu Robotics’ abductive learning model allows the robot to learn a new task from as few as ten operator demonstrations, while keeping the explainability required for industrial safety and the 99%+ accuracy that production lines demand.

“When we launched Entourage two years ago, we had a simple ambition: to back the next generation of legendary founders. We wrote the first cheques into companies like Aikido, Conveo and Lexroom. According to him, this experience helped forge Entourage’s approach: build conviction, invest early and keep founders firmly in the driver’s seat.

Once the content is created, training can be delivered via a web browser, mobile devices, or fully immersive XR headsets such as Meta Quest. The results are tracked centrally, and content can be updated and redeployed across an organisation at any time.

The raise marks the company’s first external capital since it was founded in 2023 and was led by London-based Octopus Ventures. KPN Ventures, the strategic investment arm of Dutch telecom operator KPN, also participated in the round.

“The best infrastructure businesses make something complex feel effortless. Jignesh and the Braid team have taken an industry built around long negotiations and fragmented systems and created a materially simpler way for businesses to embed connectivity into the products their customers already use. We believe Braid is defining a new category in embedded connectivity and has the team, technology and ambition to become the default infrastructure layer for businesses delivering connectivity to their customers,” said Uthish Ranjan, Partner at Octopus Ventures.

As part of this funding announcement, the company rebranded from Next Communications and claims to serve close to 90 enterprise customers, including major global FinTech and travel brands.

Before starting Braid, Jignesh Dave spent years in the UK and South African banking, including a stint at Lloyds, before building and running a mobile virtual network operator (MVNO) for seven years. That experience, which cost him €500k and 18 months of runway before a single SIM was sold, became the bedrock of Braid’s foundation: infrastructure beneath a connectivity business is more valuable than the SIM card itself.

Braid offers a single API that orchestrates more than 600 carrier networks across over 200 countries, allowing enterprises to embed SIM and eSIM connectivity directly into their own products, or launch fully branded storefronts without becoming telecom operators themselves.

Its API shrinks months of carrier negotiations, regulatory filings and procurement down to minutes. The company says live trials can be up and running in three minutes and a brand-led mobile launch in as little as a week.

“I spent 18 months and half a million euros just to sell my first SIM card, and that is why Braid exists. After seven years running a mobile virtual network, I realised we weren’t really selling SIM cards. We had built the infrastructure that makes connectivity accessible to everyone,” Jignesh Dave, co-founder and CEO of Braid.

He added, “Amazon built AWS to power its own business and found it could power everyone else’s, and it was the same for us. Today a business can start in three minutes. And when brands make connectivity part of their customer experience, they unlock something far more valuable: stronger relationships, greater loyalty and new revenue.”

In practice, Braid helps an airline offer seamless roaming from the moment a passenger books a ticket; a bank can reward customers with connectivity as a loyalty benefit; a sports club can keep fans connected when they travel abroad for matches.

Braid says the company has been profitable and cash-flow positive and plans to use the new capital for international expansion, deepen the company’s carrier network, and strengthen the infrastructure that underpins its growing position in embedded connectivity. In the long term, Braid sees itself becoming the default infrastructure for enterprise connectivity globally.

]]> German startups are increasingly looking towards Japan as a destination for international expansion, industrial partnerships and technological cooperation.

From DefenceTech and nuclear fusion to quantum computing and space infrastructure, recent developments suggest that Tokyo is becoming an important partner for some of Europe’s most ambitious technology companies.

This momentum became particularly visible today, during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Japan. Munich-based Proxima Fusion announced two Japanese partnerships, while drone manufacturer Quantum Systems unveiled agreements with Mitsubishi Chemical and Panasonic, alongside plans to establish a permanent presence in Tokyo.

The announcements form part of a wider diplomatic push. According to Japanese news agency Jiji Press, Germany and Japan were expected to sign 33 memoranda of understanding (MoUs) spanning AI, nuclear fusion and other advanced technologies.

However, the more interesting story for Europe’s startup ecosystem extends beyond a single diplomatic visit.

More than handshakes

For Quantum Systems, the visit marks a step towards becoming an established player in Japan’s DefenceTech market.

Founded in 2015 in Gilching by Florian Seibel, Michael Kriegel, Tobias Kloss and Armin Busse, Quantum Systems develops unmanned aerial systems and software for defence, security and civilian applications.

The company announced the establishment of Quantum Systems Japan K.K., including a Tokyo office, alongside MoUs with Mitsubishi Chemical and Panasonic. The agreements aim to combine Japanese manufacturing capabilities with German drone technology, strengthening local supply chains and bringing Quantum Systems closer to Japanese customers.

Sven Kruck, co-CEO of Quantum Systems, said: “Japan has understood where defence is heading: unmanned systems, rapid innovation and the industrial capacity to deliver at scale. Ukraine has shown why this matters. When personnel are scarce and threats evolve fast, technological advantage is decisive. Japan’s manufacturing strength and our operational experience are a powerful combination. We are proud to put down roots in Japan and honoured to help strengthen its defence industrial base.”

Meanwhile, Munich-based Proxima Fusion, founded in 2023 as a spin-out from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, announced two separate agreements involving fusion energy.

As EU-Startups reported earlier today, its agreement with Kyoto Fusioneering focuses on plasma-heating systems and fuel-cycle technologies. A separate agreement with Fujikura explores industrial-scale manufacturing of superconducting tape in Lower Saxony, building on a previously announced €140 million manufacturing initiative.

The cooperation also extends into space. Established German aerospace group OHB signed an MoU with Japanese space-tech company Astroscale, founded in 2013, to explore opportunities in orbital servicing, surveillance and space security. Astroscale, on the same day, also announced a €17 million (£15 million) MOD Contract from the UK Government.

Tokyo was already calling

The latest announcements are part of a broader trend we’v seen here at EU-Startups.

Munich-based defence AI startup Helsing, founded in 2021, has already been pursuing opportunities in Japan. In August 2026, Reuters reported that Japanese conglomerate Rakuten was helping Helsing pursue a potential contract to supply unmanned systems to Japan’s military. Its HX-2 strike drone was undergoing testing by Japan’s Ground Self-Defence Forces.

Industrial cooperation has also attracted Japanese capital into Germany. In March 2025, Panasonic announced a €30 million equity investment in Munich-based tado°, founded in 2011, expanding an existing partnership combining Panasonic’s heat pumps with tado°’s smart heating controls and energy management software.

Quantum computing provides another example. Braunschweig-based QUDORA Technologies, founded in 2021, established a Japanese subsidiary and partnered with Fixstars in May 2026 to make its quantum computing tools accessible through a cloud platform.

By October, QUDORA Japan had been selected for a government-backed research project alongside Kyocera and Japan’s National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology.

Even outside DeepTech, German companies have recognised the opportunity. Cologne-based translation technology company DeepL, founded in 2017, established a Japanese subsidiary in 2023 to strengthen its local commercial operations.

These developments suggest that Japanese partnerships are becoming an increasingly deliberate part of German startups’ international strategies.

Why Japan, why now?

Japan’s strengths in electronics, robotics, precision engineering, advanced materials and industrial manufacturing offer European startups capabilities that can be difficult and expensive to develop independently.

For companies building fusion reactors, quantum computers or advanced robotics, access to established manufacturers and specialised suppliers may be just as valuable as attracting new customers.

Japan has also been working to strengthen its startup ecosystem. Its five-year startup development plan, introduced in 2022, set an ambitious objective of increasing annual startup investment to approximately €56 billion (¥10 trillion) by the 2027 financial year.

Meanwhile, cooperation between Brussels and Tokyo is expanding. In May 2026, the EU and Japan agreed to deepen collaboration in AI, quantum technology, semiconductors, digital infrastructure and cross-border data flows.

The Tokyo test

Despite the momentum, Japan is not necessarily an easy market to enter.

Language barriers, different business practices, complex procurement processes and the importance of long-term corporate relationships can make expansion challenging, particularly for startups with limited resources.

The experiences of Quantum Systems, Helsing and QUDORA highlight one possible solution: finding established Japanese partners rather than attempting to navigate the market independently.

German startups appear to have recognised the opportunity Japan offers foreign tech and talent. The question now is whether the rest of Europe will follow.

The post First look at Perth Airport’s new terminal designed by Western Sydney’s architects appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • Perth Airport has unveiled designs for a 159,000sqm terminal by Woods Bagot, also the architects behind Western Sydney International Airport.
  • The terminal will feature 22 contact gates and bring Qantas domestic and international operations into one precinct, making connections easier.
  • It forms part of the multi-billion-dollar One Airport project, although firm terminal costs and completion dates remain unconfirmed.

A new 159,000sqm terminal is the centrepiece of Perth Airport’s multi-billion-dollar One Airport project, with the lead architect also behind the design of Western Sydney International Airport.

Perth Airport has released updated concept designs for its new terminal that would bring the airport’s four terminals together in one precinct. The designs draw on Western Australia’s landscape and Whadjuk Noongar Country.

The new terminal is the centrepiece of a broader multi-billion-dollar One Airport transformation programme. It will consolidate airport operations and make Qantas a central hub, under a deal signed with the Australian flag-carrier in 2024. Currently, Perth’s international and domestic terminals sit about 12km apart, with passengers transferring between them by complimentary shuttle bus or taxi.

Perth Airport’s new terminal targets growth to 30.8 million passengers

Perth recorded a record 18.4 million passengers in FY2026, including 5.5 million international travellers. The airport expects that total figure to reach 30.8 million over the next 20 years.

The terminal is designed to facilitate that growth. At 159,000 sqm, it is nearly triple the size of Terminals 3 and 4 and 25% larger than the combined size of Terminals 1 and 2. It will have 22 contact gates for wide- and narrow-body aircraft, including ‘swing gates’ that can switch between international and domestic use.

Passengers will benefit from 22 new contact gates to accommodate a variety of wide- and narrow-body aircraft. The new gates will include “swing gates” that can switch between international and domestic operations, as needed.

“Ultimately, the New Terminal will strengthen Perth’s position as Australia’s western gateway and generate new opportunities for the state,” said Perth Airport CEO, Jason Waters.

Inside Woods Bagot’s design for Perth Airport’s new terminal

The designs were developed with Australian architecture firm Woods Bagot. The “Big Sky/ Deep Earth” theme draws on the relationship between Western Australia’s vast sky and the ancient land of Whadjuk Noongar Country.

The architects say they have embedded cultural knowledge, local landscapes, climate and light into the building, with sustainability and accessibility for all central to the design.

“A good airport moves passengers efficiently, but a great airport also gives them a sense of the destination they are in,” continued Waters. The designs for the new terminal, he continued, “deliver both outcomes.”

New runway, hotel and roads form wider One Airport project

Perth’s One Airport project also includes a new parallel runway, two multi-storey car parks with associated roadworks, an upgrade of Terminal 2 and the airport’s first hotel.

Perth Airport’s property arm, Skyfields, is overseeing 250 hectares of developable land across the 2.015-hectare Airport Estate. The land is earmarked for business, lifestyle and leisure developments 15 minutes from the Perth Central Business District.

The airport currently generates around $6.6 billion a year in economic benefit for Western Australia. The airport forecasts that figure will rise to about $18 billion a year by 2046.  Currently, around 95% of visitors to the state arrive by air.

“My government remains focused on growing aviation capacity and working closely with Perth Airport and airline partners to expand our tourism sector, as part of our work to diversify the economy and create more local jobs for Western Australians,” said Western Australian Premier Roger Cook.

The architects behind Western Sydney International Airport

Woods Bagot was also the lead architect on Western Sydney International Airport, which welcomed its first passengers on 25 October. WSI was designed as a relief valve for Sydney’s Kingsford Smith Airport. Woods Bagot worked with builder Multiplex to develop the reference design by ZHA Architects and COX Architecture into the finished terminal.

Woods Bagot CEO Sarah Key, who was also the project director, described the airport as a “front door for Western Sydney’s two million residents and for everyone behind it. For a lot of people, it will be where they say goodbye and where they come home.”

The design draws on the Cumberland Plain, the Blue Mountains, local waterways and the stories of Dharug Country, with sandstone walls and an ochre and earth-tone palette.

“One of the great risks on a project of this scale is that it starts to lose its connection to place,” said Neil Hill, Woods Bagot Principal and WSI lead architect.

“Our role was making sure that relationship remained visible in the details, the materials, the views and the experience of moving through the building.”

Qantas consolidation promises easier connections at Perth Airport

WSI sets a benchmark for Perth. Australia now has a curfew-free airport with domestic and international gates under one terminal roof, and airlines are weighing up where to put new capacity. Carriers including Singapore Airlines, Air New Zealand, Jetstar and Qantas have already committed to WSI. It signals sustained confidence in Australia-bound long-haul demand.

Perth is pitching for a share of that growth. A seamless connecting hub on Australia’s west coast would appeal to airlines and passengers alike. Qantas already has plans to move all services from Terminals 3 and 4 into the new terminal.

However, there is a caveat. Perth’s consolidation has been discussed for decades and has been delayed by obstacles, including the COVID-19 pandemic. Waters has not disclosed firm timelines or costs of the new terminal. He has indicated that preliminary work could begin within 12 months, but he has also warned travellers to expect disruption during the construction period, according to ABC.

With WSI already open, Perth is playing catch-up, even though its long-term plan is well aligned with where the industry is heading.

The post Alaska Airlines to launch nonstop Boeing 737 Anchorage–Tokyo service appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • Alaska Airlines will launch nonstop Anchorage–Tokyo Narita flights on 13 May 2027, using Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft.
  • Flights will operate daily through early September, with three-times-weekly winter service beginning in January 2028.
  • The airline says the MAX 8 is its only fleet variant with sufficient range for the route; its first larger MAX 10 is expected in Q2 2027.

Alaska Airlines will establish its first nonstop link between Anchorage and Tokyo in May 2027, as the US carrier continues with its expansion plan – this time across the Pacific.

The service to Tokyo Narita will begin on 13 May 2027, initially operating daily through the summer before switching to three flights a week from January 2028. 

Alaska Airlines uses the MAX 8 for its trans-Pacific crossing

The route will be flown by Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, making Alaska the only US domestic carrier operating scheduled services to Tokyo with the narrowbody type from Anchorage.

The MAX 8, with its superior range, is being used in favour of the newly-certified MAX 10. The carrier expects to receive its first Boeing 737 MAX 10 delivery next spring, following the aircraft’s FAA type approval earlier this month. 

The launch marks a new direct connection between Alaska and the hugely popular Japanese capital, supporting both tourism and commercial links from the major US cargo hub. 

The airline said it would also give travellers from Japan easier access to destinations across Alaska, including Denali National Park and areas known for viewing the northern lights.

Expanding its Anchorage network east and west

The Tokyo route is part of what Alaska Airlines describes as its largest-ever nonstop schedule from Anchorage, with additional seasonal services to Austin, Nashville and Dallas-Fort Worth planned for 2027.

The new domestic routes will improve connections between Alaska and major US cities.

Alaska Airlines regional vice president Marilyn Romano said the link with Japan had been requested for some time. The airline has served communities in Alaska since 1932 and will mark its 95th anniversary next year.

“Our ambitions are global, but our foundation remains the same. From the beginning, Alaska Airlines has connected communities across Alaska, the West Coast and beyond,” she said. “From Anchorage to Tokyo and destinations around the globe, we’re building on that legacy and giving our guests more ways to explore the world with Alaska Airlines.”

Last week, Alaska announced it was broadening its network from Seattle, launching nonstop services to Osaka and Tahiti in 2027 using Hawaiian Airlines aircraft.

From spring next year, Alaska Airlines will offer the only nonstop service between Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Osaka in Japan and Papeete in Tahiti, French Polynesia.

Following its 2024 acquisition of Hawaiian Airlines, Alaska Airlines is deploying the carrier’s Airbus A330-200 aircraft on both routes, providing convenient connections across the two airlines’ combined networks.

Boeing 737 MAX 8 offers the range needed to reach Japan

Alaska will use the 737 MAX 8 on the Anchorage–Tokyo route. The airline says the aircraft has greater range than the larger Boeing 737 MAX 10 and is the only variant in its fleet capable of operating the service without a stopover.

The airline says passengers will have First Class, Premium Class and Main Cabin seats to choose from. First Class includes recliner seating and multi-course dining, while Premium Class and Main Cabin passengers will receive complimentary meals. Wi-Fi is also being introduced across Alaska’s MAX 8 fleet with the installation of Starlink.

The Anchorage expansion comes as Alaska Airlines continues to develop its wider network across North America, Latin America, Asia, the Pacific and Europe. 

The airline operates alongside Hawaiian Airlines and Horizon Air within Alaska Air Group, with Alaska and Hawaiian both members of the Oneworld alliance.

The Tokyo service is scheduled to run daily during its initial summer period, with the last departure from Anchorage on 7 September and the final return flight from Tokyo on 8 September 2027. 

Three-times-a-week winter operations are due to begin in January 2028.

Read more: Alaska Airlines expands long-haul network as the sole carrier serving Osaka and Tahiti from Seattle Read more: Alaska Airlines expands long-haul network as the sole carrier serving Osaka and Tahiti from Seattle

Alaska awaits the MAX 10

Alaska Airlines welcomed the FAA’s certification of the Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft last week, calling it a “pivotal milestone [which] opens new possibilities”.

“The MAX 10 is an important part of Alaska’s long-term fleet strategy and our future,” said Alaska Air Group CEO Ben Minicucci. “These modern, fuel-efficient airplanes will help us connect more people to more of the world, and on at least 25 of them, our new Aurora lie-flat suites will raise the bar for comfort on transcontinental flights. 

“Certification of the MAX 10 has been a rigorous, deliberate process, and we respect the work the FAA and Boeing have put into it. We appreciate the thoroughness of the agency’s review, and we’re grateful to Boeing for its effort in bringing this vision to life.”

Alaska says the MAX 10’s “additional capacity and improved per-seat economics can serve high-demand routes more efficiently while managing fuel use and emissions”.

In January, Alaska announced its largest order in the company’s history for 105 additional MAX 10s. 

Alaska has firm orders for 168 aircraft across the MAX family, with most of those orders for the MAX 10. 

Alaska’s transcontinental MAX 10 will have 12 new Aurora Suites on at least 25 aircraft, the first time in the carrier’s history that lie-flat seating will be available on its 737 fleet.

Alaska currently expects delivery of its first MAX 10 in the second quarter of 2027.

]]> Ethiopia receives Russian Su-35 fighters a year early, with S-400s set to follow https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ethiopia-su-35-fighters-delivery-s-400/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:32:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54850 Ethiopia has taken a surprise delivery of Russian Su-35S fighter jets, confirming a 2025 Black Mirror leak.

The post Ethiopia receives Russian Su-35 fighters a year early, with S-400s set to follow appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • Ethiopia says deliveries under its 12-aircraft Su-35 order have arrived a year early, although the number received remains unclear.
  • Russian S-400 air defence systems are also expected, as tensions with neighbouring Eritrea and Egypt remain high.
  • The fighters’ origins and any US sanctions response remain uncertain, including whether Ethiopia received aircraft originally built for Egypt.

Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said yesterday that the country has received its order for 12 Russian Sukhoi Su-35S air superiority fighters. There is some confusion over whether the delivery was a batch of the 12 ordered, or the whole group of 12.

Ethiopia takes delivery of first Su-35S fighter jets

According to reporting by Reuters, Ahmed said that the Su-35S deliveries are a year early and that Ethiopia would also be receiving Russian S-400 air defence systems later on.

The announcement comes as federal Ethiopian forces launch an offensive in the northern Tigray region and tensions with neighbouring Eritrea are at a very high level.

The broader Ethiopian geopolitical context is extremely complicated. Reuters has reported that Ethiopia hosted a secret camp to train fighters for Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), although Addis Ababa has denied involvement.

Ethiopia’s relationship with Egypt is likewise tense, with Cairo previously threatening to bomb the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile. Egypt is again furious with Ethiopia as it plans to build more dams on the Nile, with some Egyptian politicians threatening military action.

S-400s and Su-35S could plausibly allow Ethiopia to better protect its dams on the Nile, while also helping to tilt the balance of power with Eritrea more in its favour.

The 2025 Black Mirror leak

In October 2025, AGN reported on a leak by Black Mirror that showed Su-35 fighter jet sales to Algeria, Iran, and Ethiopia, with Su-57 fighter jets also sold to Algeria.

One year on, the Su-35S and Su-57s are being delivered to Algeria, and the first Su-35S deliveries to Ethiopia have been officially announced. However, earlier reported deliveries of Su-35S fighter jets to Iran have not materialized, and the type was apparently absent from the 2026 war.

Confirmation on what I was the first to report on Aug 2022 about the contract between Iran and Russia for the purchase of Su-35 fighters. The contract includes 48 Su-35 fighters for 2026-2028. H/t: @GeorgeN28581 https://t.co/AubCzgGzNX

— Mehdi H. (@mhmiranusa) October 3, 2025

The leaked document showed 48 Su-35 fighter jet sales to Iran (listed as “364”), 12 Su-57 and 14 Su-34 fighter jet sales to Algeria (listed as “012”), and six Su-35s for Ethiopia (listed as “231”). It appears the number for Algeria has since grown to 12.

First Su-57E Felon Russian fighter jets spotted flying in Algeria First Su-57E Felon Russian fighter jets spotted flying in Algeria

CAATSA and the ex-Egyptian pool of Su-35s

The US’s CAATSA act sanctions countries purchasing significant weapons (e.g., fighter jets) from Russia, Iran, and North Korea. The act pressured countries to cancel or abandon contracts and plans to purchase Russian fighter jets and helicopters.

Egypt had contracted to purchase Su-35s, and around 24 examples had been built when Egypt canceled the contract. This left Russia stranded with aircraft without a customer.

Some of these appear to have been sold to Algeria, with fighter jets delivered still displaying Egyptian camouflage paint. More ex-Egyptian planes were reported to have been earmarked for Iran, but following Operation Epic Fury, the status of that is unclear.

Interesting report indicating Algeria has purchased at least some of the Russian Su-35s originally built for Egypt and later reported to be sought by Iran. https://t.co/0soV9aOopn

— John Hardie (@JohnH105) April 9, 2025

It is unknown if some or all of the Ethiopian Su-35S fighter jets are new-builds specifically for Ethiopia or if they are from the pool of aircraft built for Egypt. Ethiopia signed an initial contract for six examples in 2022, after Egypt had pulled the plug on the Flankers.

Given the tensions between Egypt and Ethiopia, there would be some degree of irony if they are Flankers originally built for Egypt.

It is also unclear if the purchase of Su-35Ss and S-400s will trigger US sanctions under CAATSA. The US successfully pressured Egypt, the Philippines, and Indonesia to abandon plans to purchase Russian fighters and helicopters.

The US has carved out a special exemption for India and seemingly turned a blind eye to Algeria. It remains to be seen if the US will take action against Ethiopia.

]]> Air France cancels Dubai and Riyadh flights for weeks more as suspensions extended https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/air-france-riyadh-dubai-flight-cancellations/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:19:59 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54945 Air France has extended cancellations on its Riyadh and Dubai routes. Here are the latest dates, other airline suspensions and passenger options.

The post Air France cancels Dubai and Riyadh flights for weeks more as suspensions extended appeared first on AGN.

]]> Air France has extended the suspension of flights to and from Dubai until 7 November and Riyadh until 12 December 2026, prolonging disruption for passengers travelling between France and the Gulf.

The latest extension, announced on Thursday, 29 October, comes as security concerns continue to affect airline operations across the Middle East. The restrictions cover the French carrier’s services to both destinations, with passengers facing further changes to travel plans as airlines reassess their schedules.

The dates mark the end of the currently announced cancellation periods. They do not guarantee that flights will resume immediately afterwards.

Air France Dubai and Riyadh suspensions extended

Air France first cancelled flights to Dubai and Riyadh on 28 February 2026, following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and the closure of airspace across parts of the region.

The airline has subsequently issued repeated updates as the security situation has evolved. Its March schedule announcement confirmed that both destinations remained suspended at that point, while additional capacity was being deployed to alternative markets in Asia.

More recently, Reuters reported on 20 October that Riyadh services were suspended through 7 November, while Dubai flights remained cancelled through 31 October. Today’s announcement pushes both deadlines further back.

Passengers should check their individual bookings rather than assume that every flight after the published suspension deadline will operate.

Other airlines extend Middle East flight cancellations

Air France’s decision follows extensions announced by several other airlines in recent days and weeks. The measures vary by carrier and destination and were not all announced on 29 October.

These are airline-specific restrictions. A suspended service does not necessarily mean that the destination airport is closed or that other carriers have stopped operating.

What to do if your flight is cancelled

Check your flight status and booking before leaving for the airport. Contact the operating airline, or your travel agent if you booked through one, to discuss the available alternatives.

For flights covered by EU passenger-rights rules, including Air France-operated services between France and these destinations, passengers whose flights are cancelled can choose between a refund and rerouting. Rerouting can be at the earliest opportunity or at a later convenient date, subject to seat availability.

Passengers awaiting the earliest available alternative may also be entitled to meals, refreshments and, where necessary, accommodation and transport between the airport and hotel. Keep receipts for reasonable expenses if the airline does not provide assistance.

Security risks and airspace restrictions can constitute extraordinary circumstances, meaning additional fixed compensation may not be payable. However, that does not remove the airline’s obligations to offer refunds or rerouting and applicable care.

Before accepting a refund, consider whether you still need the airline to arrange an alternative journey: choosing reimbursement generally ends the entitlement to rerouting under those rules.

]]> Airbus maintains 870-aircraft delivery target as orders and profits rise https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/airbus-results-nine-months-2026/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:01:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54869 Despite complex geopolitical and operating environments, Airbus said it remains focused on increasing production, meeting delivery commitments and maintaining quality.

The post Airbus maintains 870-aircraft delivery target as orders and profits rise appeared first on AGN.

]]> Airbus has reported higher revenues, increased profits and a significant rise in commercial aircraft orders for the first nine months of 2026, while maintaining its full-year financial and delivery targets.

The European aerospace manufacturer has reported consolidated revenues of €50.6 billion for the nine months ended 30 September 2026, an increase of 7% compared with the same period last year.

The company delivered 547 commercial aircraft and recorded strong demand across its commercial aviation, helicopter, defence and space businesses.

Despite a complex geopolitical and operating environment, Airbus said it remains focused on increasing production, meeting delivery commitments and maintaining product quality.

Commercial aircraft orders more than double

Airbus recorded 1,174 gross commercial aircraft orders during the first nine months of this year, compared with 610 in the same period of 2025. Net orders, after cancellations, reached 1,105 aircraft, up from 514 a year earlier.

The commercial aircraft order backlog stood at 9,310 aircraft at the end of September, reflecting sustained demand for the company’s products.

Airbus Helicopters also reported positive order momentum, securing 311 net orders compared with 306 in the previous year. Its backlog reached 1,122 helicopters.

Meanwhile, Airbus Defence and Space recorded strong commercial momentum, with order intake increasing to €11.5 billion from €6.8 billion in the first nine months of 2025.

Also read: Atlantic Airways orders two more A320neos with Paris and London expansion in sight Also read: Atlantic Airways orders two more A320neos with Paris and London expansion in sight

Aircraft deliveries drive revenue growth

Airbus delivered 547 commercial aircraft during the reporting period, up from 507 in the previous year. Deliveries comprised 68 A220s, 428 A320 Family aircraft, 13 A330s and 38 A350s.

Revenue from commercial aircraft activities rose 8% to €36.7 billion, supported by higher deliveries and increased services, although the company reported that a weaker US dollar partially offset the growth.

Airbus Helicopters delivered 226 units, compared with 218 in the same period of 2025. Revenue remained broadly stable at €5.6 billion, reflecting a less favourable delivery mix.

Revenue at Airbus Defence and Space increased by 5% to €9.3 billion, driven by higher volumes across all business units.

Profitability improves across the group

Consolidated adjusted earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT Adjusted), a key indicator of underlying operating performance, increased 8% to €4.5 billion, compared with €4.1 billion in the first nine months of 2025.

Adjusted EBIT from commercial aircraft activities rose to €3.36 billion from €3.27 billion. Higher deliveries supported the improvement, although increased research and development expenditure and a less favourable hedging rate partially offset the gains.

Airbus Helicopters recorded adjusted EBIT of €445 million, down from €495 million, reflecting its less favourable delivery mix.

In contrast, Airbus Defence and Space reported a substantial improvement in adjusted EBIT, which increased to €672 million from €420 million. Higher volumes and improved profitability across its business units supported the increase.

Group research and development expenditure rose to €2.33 billion from €2.15 billion, reflecting continued investment in technology and product development. Reported EBIT increased 35% to €4.55 billion, while consolidated net income climbed 36% to €3.59 billion. Reported earnings per share rose to €4.54 from €3.34.

Also read: Airbus predicts demand for 2,670 freighters as global air cargo fleet grows 46% Also read: Airbus predicts demand for 2,670 freighters as global air cargo fleet grows 46%

Cash flow and financial position

Airbus reported free cash flow before customer financing of negative €1.27 billion, compared with negative €914 million a year earlier. Total free cash flow was negative €1.11 billion, against negative €778 million in the same period of 2025.

The cash outflow mainly reflected working capital changes, including inventory build-up tied to a back-end-loaded delivery schedule and planned production increases across the business.

At the end of September 2026, Airbus held a gross cash position of €21.9 billion and a net cash position of €7.0 billion, compared with €27.2 billion and €12.2 billion, respectively, at the end of 2025.

Production ramp-up plans remain on track

Airbus continues to progress its commercial aircraft production ramp-up plans. The company is targeting a monthly production rate of 13 A220 aircraft in 2028. For the A320 Family, it expects to reach a monthly rate of between 70 and 75 aircraft by the end of 2027, stabilising at 75 thereafter.

Airbus also continues to target a production rate of five A330 aircraft per month in 2029 and 12 A350 aircraft per month in 2028.

CEO Guillaume Faury said the results reflected the upward trajectory of the company’s civil and military production ramp-up, supported by strong demand across its portfolio. He highlighted delivery performance and product quality as priorities amid ongoing geopolitical and operational challenges.

Airbus maintains 2026 financial guidance

Airbus has maintained its full-year 2026 guidance, assuming no additional disruptions to global trade, the wider economy, air traffic, supply chains, internal operations or its ability to deliver products and services.

The company’s targets remain at approximately 870 commercial aircraft deliveries by the end of the year and an adjusted EBIT of approximately €7.5 billion.

Free cash flow before customer financing is forecast to reach approximately €4.5 billion. The guidance is before mergers and acquisitions and includes the impact of currently applicable tariffs.

With strong order intake, higher nine-month revenues and improved reported profitability, Airbus continues to focus on production growth and delivery performance as it works towards its full-year objectives.

  • The experimental jet has completed 40 additional flights since its maiden flight a year ago, reaching Mach 1.53 and exceeding 56,000 feet.
  • Upcoming noise measurements and community surveys will help regulators assess whether quieter supersonic passenger flights could be permitted over land.

NASA‘s experimental X-59 supersonic aircraft is making its first cross-country journey to Kennedy Space Centre in Florida as the agency celebrates the first anniversary of the jet’s maiden flight.

The aircraft departed California on 28 October 2026, exactly one year after its first flight. It made stops in El Paso and Fort Worth, Texas, on its way to the Sunshine State. It is expected to appear at NASA’s MAX POWER airshow at Kennedy Space Centre on 7–8 November, taking part in celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of American independence.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman confirmed the aircraft was heading to Kennedy Space Center in a reply to a post on X by an aviation enthusiast who captured the aircraft in flight over Fort Worth on  Wednesday.

@LensOfMae @thenewarea51 @gfontana767 Great catch… X-59 making her way to @NASAKennedy

— NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman (@NASAAdmin) October 28, 2026

The X-59 landed at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on 28 October, accompanied by a NASA F-15 safety chase aircraft. A NASA F/A-18 and Gulfstream C-20 were also tracked along the route.

NASA reports significant progress in testing the aircraft, which is designed to demonstrate that supersonic flight is possible without the disruptive sonic booms created by aircraft travelling faster than sound. 

X-59 completes 40 flights in its first year

According to NASA’s anniversary update, the X-59 has completed 40 additional flights since its maiden flight on 28 October 2025.

That first flight, piloted by NASA test pilot Nils Larson, lasted 67 minutes and focused on basic handling characteristics and aircraft systems.

The aircraft has since exceeded 56,000 feet and reached a maximum speed of Mach 1.53, approximately 1,010 mph.

On 5 June 2026, the X-59 exceeded the speed of sound for the first time, reaching Mach 1.1 at 43,400 feet. A week later, it achieved its intended operating conditions of Mach 1.4 at 55,000 feet.

Testing continued through the summer, including six flights over three days in September. NASA test pilot Mike Lippert completed his first flight in the aircraft on 21 October.

The flights have allowed engineers to expand the aircraft’s operating envelope, assessing its handling and performance at progressively higher speeds and altitudes. 

X-59 to appear at NASA’s MAX POWER airshow

The aircraft’s journey to Florida will bring it to NASA’s MAX POWER aerospace expo and airshow, scheduled for 7–8 November at Kennedy Space Centre. The agency has not specified whether the aircraft will perform a flying demonstration or appear as a static display.

The airshow will feature NASA aircraft, the US Air Force Thunderbirds and other military aviation displays. Visitors can see new aerospace technologies, including autonomous aircraft, drones and spacecraft.

The X-59’s appearance will let visitors see an aircraft that has spent most of its flight-testing programme operating from California. 

Could the X-59 make supersonic passenger flights quieter?

The X-59 was developed by Lockheed Martin‘s Skunk Works division for NASA’s Quesst mission, which aims to provide evidence that could support the return of commercial supersonic flights over land.

Conventional supersonic aircraft produce loud sonic booms when shockwaves generated by their passage through the air reach the ground. The X-59’s long, narrow nose and specially shaped fuselage are designed to prevent those shockwaves from combining into a powerful boom.

NASA expects the aircraft to produce a much quieter sound, comparable to a car door closing from around 20 feet away, when flying at its intended test conditions of Mach 1.4 and 55,000 feet.

The next major stage of testing will involve acoustic validation, during which NASA will measure the sound produced by the aircraft during supersonic flight.

The agency then plans to fly the X-59 over selected communities in the United States and survey residents about the noise they experience.

NASA will share results with aviation regulators, including the Federal Aviation Administration, to help them assess whether new noise standards could allow commercial supersonic operations over land.

The X-59 is a research aircraft, not a prototype passenger jet, but the technical and public-response data it helps collect could determine whether quieter supersonic aircraft could operate commercially in future.

In Brief 4 min read
  • New photographs appear to show a full-sized COMAC CE-25A demonstrator, although their authenticity and the aircraft’s flight status remain unconfirmed.
  • The proposed 19-seat all-electric commuter aircraft features 10 wing-integrated ducted fans and targets a range of 400–500 km.
  • Battery performance, payload, charging infrastructure and certification remain key hurdles, with no confirmed commercial service timeline.

New photographs appear to show a full-sized demonstrator of China’s CE-25A, an unusual 19-seat all-electric commuter aircraft designed for short- and medium-distance passenger transport.

Developed by state-owned aircraft manufacturer COMAC, the project showcases China’s ambitions to explore new approaches to electric aviation. However, questions remain over the demonstrator’s authenticity, flight status, and future role.

COMAC presents its first CE-25A demonstrator

Images circulating online appear to offer the clearest look yet at the CE-25A, an unconventional aircraft developed by the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC).

The photographs, reportedly shared by Chinese automotive blogger Han Lu on 28 October, show a red-and-black aircraft featuring COMAC and CE-25A markings.

Although the images appear plausible, their authenticity has not been conclusively established. It is also unclear whether the aircraft shown has flown or exactly how it fits into the programme’s development timeline.

What is the COMAC CE-25A?

First publicly presented at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, the CE-25A is a proposed 19-seat, all-electric commuter aircraft intended for short- and medium-distance passenger transportation and business aviation.

The concept targets a market where smaller aircraft could connect regional destinations and provide point-to-point travel over relatively short distances. Its compact passenger capacity and proposed performance place it broadly within the regional commuter aircraft category.

According to previously published design specifications, the CE-25A is intended to achieve a cruising speed of approximately 400 kilometres per hour (248 mph) and a range of around 400 to 500 kilometres (250 to 310 miles).

These figures remain design targets rather than independently verified performance results for the aircraft shown in the photographs.

An unconventional all-electric propulsion system

The CE-25A’s most distinctive feature is its distributed electric propulsion system. Rather than using conventional turboprop engines, the aircraft is designed around 10 electrically driven ducted fans integrated into its wings.

This arrangement sets it apart from more conventional commuter aircraft, which typically rely on a smaller number of propellers driven by turbine engines.

Distributed electric propulsion offers designers new possibilities for integrating thrust generation with the aircraft’s aerodynamic design.

Depending on the configuration, multiple propulsion units could help improve aerodynamic efficiency and performance in particular flight conditions.

Electric motors can also offer mechanical simplicity compared with conventional turbine engines, potentially reducing some maintenance requirements.

Crucially, the CE-25A is described as an all-electric aircraft, meaning its intended propulsion system does not rely on conventional aviation fuel-burning engines.

However, its detailed battery configuration, energy-storage capacity, and charging requirements have not been fully established in publicly available information.

The challenges facing electric aviation

Despite the potential benefits, developing an all-electric passenger aircraft presents significant engineering challenges.

Batteries currently store considerably less energy per unit of weight than conventional aviation fuel. This places limitations on an aircraft’s range, payload and endurance, making battery technology one of the most important factors determining whether electric commuter aircraft can become commercially viable.

High-power electrical systems also require effective thermal management, while operating 10 separate propulsion units introduces additional considerations involving reliability, maintenance and flight control.

The CE-25A’s proposed range could make it suitable for relatively short regional journeys if its design targets are achieved.

Nevertheless, commercial viability would depend on demonstrated performance, passenger and baggage payload, operating costs, charging infrastructure and regulatory approval.

What happens next with the CE-25A?

The newly surfaced images raise questions about how far the CE-25A programme has progressed. COMAC previously discussed experimental aircraft verification work involving a scaled demonstrator, but the aircraft now appearing in photographs looks full-sized.

There is no clear public confirmation that the pictured aircraft has completed a flight, and its precise role in the development programme remains uncertain.

The project also reflects wider interest in electric propulsion across the aviation industry. Research programmes in Europe and the United States have explored similar technologies, although other designs have pursued different approaches, including hybrid-electric propulsion.

For COMAC, the CE-25A provides an opportunity to investigate technologies that could influence future aircraft development, including electric motors, power distribution, thermal management and the integration of multiple propulsion units.

Whether the CE-25A eventually enters commercial service remains to be seen. In the meantime, the aircraft represents an intriguing step in China’s exploration of all-electric aviation, with its 10-fan configuration offering a distinctive alternative to conventional regional aircraft designs.

]]>
In Brief 6 min read
  • The Pentagon has released a rare, detailed image of China’s secretive Shenlong spaceplane.
  • China’s reusable spacecraft programme has attracted growing attention because of its long missions, orbital manoeuvres and ability to release objects into space.
  • Its 2026 assessment warns that China is developing weapons and other systems capable of disrupting, damaging or destroying satellites.

The Pentagon has released a rare, detailed image of China’s secretive Shenlong spaceplane, offering one of the clearest public views yet of a reusable spacecraft that has been conducting extended missions and releasing objects in orbit.

The image, captured in 2024 by US commercial satellite imagery company Maxar Technologies, now known as Vantor, appears in a new Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) report examining growing military threats to American and allied satellites.

It shows a winged spacecraft with what appear to be open payload bay doors and structures extending from either side. The vehicle bears a striking resemblance to the US Space Force’s Boeing-built X-37B, another uncrewed spaceplane whose missions remain partly classified.

China has disclosed little about Shenlong’s operations. The DIA report, Challenges to Security in Space, published on October 26, provides a closer look at the programme, including occasions when the spacecraft appeared to manoeuvre near objects it had released.

The photograph is particularly notable because detailed images of Shenlong in orbit have rarely been made public. While the vehicle’s configuration suggests it can carry payloads, the DIA report does not establish that Shenlong is armed.

What the Pentagon knows about Shenlong

China’s reusable spacecraft programme has attracted growing attention because of its long missions, orbital manoeuvres and ability to release objects into space.

The first Chinese experimental reusable spacecraft launched in September 2020 and returned to Earth after two days.

A subsequent mission, launched in August 2022, remained in orbit for 276 days. During that flight, American observers tracked an unusual encounter involving the spaceplane and another object.

“In November 2022, this spaceplane appeared to manoeuvre with a companion satellite and conduct station-keeping at around 1 kilometre separation,” the DIA report states.

At one point, the two objects appeared to approach within 100 metres. The agency says they may have rendezvoused before the smaller satellite was released again.

China launched another mission in December 2023. That spacecraft remained in orbit for 268 days and also released and interacted with an object.

Such operations demonstrate technologies relevant to satellite deployment, inspection and close-range manoeuvring.

They are also difficult to interpret from the ground. A spacecraft approaching another object might be conducting a routine experiment, testing servicing equipment or demonstrating capabilities that could eventually have military applications.

The DIA identifies Shenlong and Tengyun as China’s two principal spaceplane models. It distinguishes these from Haolong-1, a proposed cargo spaceplane intended to support China’s space station.

Reusable spaceplanes offer greater flexibility than conventional satellites because they can carry equipment into orbit, conduct experiments and return to Earth.

Shenlong’s precise payloads and the full purpose of its missions remain undisclosed.

How the X-37B Is shaping the future of the US space force

The closest American counterpart is the X-37B, a reusable orbital test vehicle developed by Boeing and operated for the US government.

Unlike China’s closely guarded Shenlong programme, the X-37B’s launch and landing history is publicly documented, although many of its experiments remain classified.

The American spacecraft first flew in April 2010 and has since completed seven missions, spending more than 4,200 cumulative days in space. Its longest flight lasted 908 days, ending in November 2022.

The seventh mission concluded on March 7, 2025, when the vehicle landed at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California after demonstrating an aerobraking manoeuvre to change its orbit while conserving propellant.

The X-37B returned to space on August 21, 2025, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for its eighth mission.

That flight carries experiments including laser communications technology and a quantum inertial sensor designed to support navigation when GPS signals are unavailable or disrupted.

The mission also uses a service module to expand the spacecraft’s capacity for experiments.

Boeing says the reusable design allows equipment to be recovered, examined and improved before another flight.

“Having a returnable space platform allows us to learn faster,” said Colonel Brian Chatman, then installation commander for Space Launch Delta 45, following the eighth mission’s launch.

“The data we gather from the X-37B speeds decisions, hardens our architectures, and helps Guardians stay connected and on course even in contested environments.”

For the Space Force, the vehicle provides a way to test technologies in actual orbital conditions without discarding the entire spacecraft after each mission.

The US Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office leads the programme, with the Space Force responsible for operations and Boeing providing the vehicle and associated support.

Although Shenlong and the X-37B share a reusable, winged configuration, their publicly disclosed missions differ considerably. The X-37B is described as an experimental test platform, while China has provided far fewer details about Shenlong’s activities.

China expands its satellite warfare capabilities

The DIA’s concerns extend well beyond Shenlong.

Its 2026 assessment warns that China is developing weapons and other systems capable of disrupting, damaging or destroying satellites, including ground-based lasers, anti-satellite missiles, cyber capabilities and spacecraft that can approach other objects in orbit.

“China has developed and will continue to advance weapons for use against satellites in orbit to disrupt, damage, and destroy other nations’ space capabilities,” the report states.

The agency says China’s military considers directed-energy weapons attractive because they can temporarily disable a satellite or cause permanent damage. Such weapons could interfere with optical sensors used for reconnaissance, preventing satellites from collecting images of military activity.

China has also demonstrated how spacecraft designed for legitimate servicing operations could acquire military significance.

In January 2022, its Shijian-21 satellite moved a defunct BeiDou navigation satellite into a higher graveyard orbit above geostationary orbit.

The DIA also identifies Shijian-17, equipped with a robotic arm, as an example of technology capable of grappling another satellite.

These systems have legitimate applications, including debris removal and satellite servicing. Their ability to approach and physically manipulate spacecraft, however, makes them relevant to military planners.

China’s 2007 anti-satellite missile test illustrates another danger. The destruction of an ageing weather satellite created thousands of pieces of debris, many of which remain in orbit.

Russia’s nuclear satellite threat

Russia presents a different and potentially more destructive challenge.

The DIA says Moscow is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon, despite the 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibiting nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in Earth orbit.

“Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty,” the report states.

The agency warns that such a capability could cause the sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites, disrupting communications, navigation, weather forecasting and military operations.

The report also identifies Russia’s Cosmos-2553, launched in February 2022 into an unusual orbit. Moscow said the spacecraft was intended to test the effects of space radiation on electronic systems.

The DIA does not establish that Cosmos-2553 itself carries a nuclear weapon.

Russia has separately demonstrated close-proximity operations involving satellites that can release smaller objects.

More recently, the Russian spacecraft Kosmos-2612 drew attention after approaching ICEYE-X36, a Finnish-operated radar imaging satellite, in October. The encounter raised concerns over uninvited manoeuvres near commercially operated spacecraft supporting military intelligence.

No hostile action against ICEYE-X36 has been publicly established.

Such incidents have helped fuel interest in bodyguard satellites, designed to monitor and potentially protect valuable spacecraft against suspicious approaches.

The UK, France, Japan and other countries are pursuing technologies relevant to this emerging field. On October 28, Astroscale UK announced a £15 million ($20 million) Ministry of Defence contract for Project LEDA, aimed at improving the UK’s understanding of orbital warfare and potentially threatening proximity operations.

The DIA report also warns that commercial satellites are becoming increasingly important to military operations. Russia’s war in Ukraine has demonstrated their value for communications and intelligence, while exposing them to electronic interference and other threats.

The British Government and engine manufacturer Rolls-Royce have agreed a jointly funded £2.5 billion, ten-year programme to develop next-generation jet engines for single-aisle passenger and military aircraft.

Ministers say the deal will keep Britain at the forefront of the global aerospace industry, while also supporting tens of thousands of jobs.

The Chancellor announced the agreement as he delivered his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October. The programme with Rolls-Royce lays out a multi-decade cooperation to develop new jet engines for single-aisle aircraft – the type that typically carry British travellers off on short- and medium-haul flights. Only a handful of nations and companies can build such engines.

Rolls-Royce reveals return to narrowbody aircraft engines

The agreement also follows Rolls-Royce’s own declaration of intent in March, when the company revealed its UltraFan 30 concept and said it was seeking up to £200 million in UK government support to help fund development and testing of the scaled demonstrator.

The geared turbofan is aimed squarely at the next generation of single-aisle aircraft, with Rolls-Royce arguing that narrowbody aircraft production is forecast to double over the next 25 years, representing a significant growth opportunity for UK aerospace manufacturing over the next half century.

Until now, the firm’s civil business has been dominated by widebody engines. The government backing provides the funding framework for that strategic shift to narrowbody engines and a clear industrial policy rationale.

Rolls-Royce says securing a UK engine on these planes could attract billions more in investment in the coming decades. It could also add £120 billion to the economy over the programme’s lifetime.

Single aisle planes to make up largest share of global civil aerospace market

Roles will range from engineering and research to manufacturing, from the design phase through to the factory floor. Officials say most of these will be outside London and the Southeast, creating employment opportunities elsewhere in the country and drawing on Rolls-Royce’s sites and supply chains nationwide.

The Aerospace Technology Institute expects the global civil aerospace market to be worth £220 billion a year by 2050, with single-aisle aircraft making up the largest share.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the deal underlined what reindustrialisation looks like in practice and gives businesses the certainty to invest. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds called it a “vote of confidence” in the Government’s economic plan and added it would ensure Britain wins the race to power the next generation of passenger planes.

Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO of Rolls-Royce, described the agreement as a “landmark moment” and a “once-in-a-generation opportunity.” He also noted it will lay the foundations for decades of sustainable economic growth across the UK, transform the country’s advanced manufacturing supply chain, and create high-value jobs.

“Aerospace is a growing and globally attractive market, and this programme with Government is vital to enable the UK to compete. During a period of growing geopolitical uncertainty and unrest, the programme will also help strengthen national security. The technologies developed, including advanced materials, electronic systems, advanced manufacturing, robotics and AI, could be applied to both civil and military engines.

The deal, which builds on a £100 million Aerospace Supply Chain fund announced this summer, also includes a commitment to ensure UK suppliers benefit directly.

Rolls-Royce spent more than £3 billion in its UK supply chain in 2025. Meanwhile, the UK aerospace sector employs around 113,000 people and contributes more than £46 billion a year to the economy.

The Government’s Industrial Strategy concludes that winning a UK-built engine on the next generation of single-aisle aircraft could be the UK aerospace sector’s biggest opportunity over the next 50 years.
